question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents say you have a duty to permit the agent's entry, but they don't say whether you must be there in person. They say nothing about a $90 rebooking fee.

**Versions applied:** Today is 3 December 2025, which falls within the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 111, and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 005. Both came into force on 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Right of entry:** A provider or agent may enter with any persons necessary for the purpose [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entry to carry out a duty under the Act requires at least 24 hours' notice, and may occur between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your 7 days' notice meets that requirement, and 10 am to 12:30 pm falls within the permitted hours. You should check that the date isn't a public holiday.
- **Smoke alarm duty:** The provider must ensure smoke alarms are tested at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). This is the kind of duty that can justify entry.
- **Notice requirements:** The notice must be in writing, state why entry is wanted, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The notice you describe appears to meet these requirements, but check the delivery method.
- **Your duty:** You have a duty to permit entry in accordance with the Division [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the renter must allow entry where the provider has followed proper procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner of entry:** The entry must be carried out in a reasonable manner and must not last longer than necessary [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The agent's key:** The documents don't address whether holding a key gives the agent any right of entry. Entry must still comply with the Division. Entering otherwise, without reasonable excuse, is an offence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to be there yourself?

The documents don't expressly say whether you must personally attend. The "must be home" condition is the agent's term, and the documents I found don't address whether a renter can arrange for someone else to provide access.

### The $90 fee

The documents I found contain no provision about a fee for rebooking an entry. The only fee provision in the retrieved text concerns consent to assignment or sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), which doesn't apply here. I can't say whether the $90 charge is lawful.

### What you can do or ask

- **Ask for a different time:** The documents don't require the agent to agree a time for a smoke alarm check. The "reasonable efforts to agree" requirement appears only for sales inspections [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). You can still ask.
- **Apply to VCAT:** You may apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying or limiting when entry may occur [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Report non-compliance:** If the provider or agent fails to follow the Division when entering, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order restraining future entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Smoke alarms:** If you find a smoke alarm that isn't working, you must notify the provider in writing as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **More information:** The Regulations point to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for more information [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the law in force on 15 January 2026, the documents indicate that the app can't charge you a card fee without your agent first telling you about it, and the agent must make a fee-free option reasonably available. The documents don't say whether it matters who receives the fee.

**What the law says**

- The governing version is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 111 (in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Version 115 applies from 13 October 2026, so it doesn't apply on your date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your bank transfer may satisfy this, though the documents don't define "reasonably available," so they don't say whether a slower method qualifies.
- The provider or agent "must give the renter information about any costs (including third party transaction fees, direct debit dishonour fees and any other electronic payment facility fees) that the renter may incur by using a particular payment method before the renter consents to use the payment method" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A payments company's card fee appears to fall within this wording.
- The duties are placed on the "residential rental provider or that person's agent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The text doesn't mention a third-party payments company, and it doesn't address whether the fee is kept by the app company or the agent.
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 005, in force 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) include a form note saying the rental provider "must permit at least one fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is a note in a form, not the operative provision, so treat it as guidance.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask your agent, in writing, what the card fee is and who charges it, and ask them to confirm the costs before you choose a payment method. The agent must give this information before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. Keep using the no-fee bank transfer. The agent must make a no-additional-cost method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. If the agent insists on card payment only, or doesn't offer a fee-free method, you could raise this with the agent in writing and seek advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT. The documents I retrieved don't set out those steps.
4. Ask for a receipt. A receipt must be given for rent, immediately for in-person payments, or within 5 business days if you request one for other payments [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether the card fee is lawful in amount, or whether the app company can charge it directly.
- Whether the payments company's arrangement with the agent changes the agent's obligations.
- What "reasonably available" means for a slower payment method.

If the agent's arrangement is central to your situation, get tailored advice from a tenancy service.

The first point is covered: it states a no-additional-cost method must be reasonably available and that 'Your bank transfer may satisfy this'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the card fee is already banned (it says only that the fee can't be charged 'without your agent first telling you about it'), and it affirms a fee-free rule exists: the agent 'must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs ... is reasonably available to the renter'.

Version 115 is mentioned only to say it does not apply yet. One problem: the Regulations form note is linked to 97-109aa110 (Act version 110), but that note repeats the fee-free rule already taken from v111, so deleting it would not change the substance.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** On 15 October 2019, the version of the Act in force was the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088 [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Under that version, you may be able to end the agreement before moving in, and the damp and mould may count as urgent repairs. The documents I retrieved do not show a right to a rent reduction for these defects.

## What the law says

- **Termination before possession:** A residential rental agreement ends if the renter has not entered into possession and gives a termination notice on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair," "unfit for human habitation," or "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp:** "Urgent repairs" include "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure," including "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure," and "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rental minimum standards:** These are the standards prescribed under section 65A of the Act [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The mould and damp standard in the current regulations requires that "each room... must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). However, that regulation text comes from a 2026 version, so it doesn't establish what the 2019 standard said.

## What you can do

1. **Cancel:** Under the 2019 Act, you can give a termination notice before moving in if the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for habitation, or don't meet the rental minimum standards [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Your situation may fit this, but "possession" is not defined in the documents. Since you have the keys but haven't moved in or stayed, get advice on whether you count as having entered possession.
2. **Ask for repairs:** Notify the provider in writing. The documents I found describe urgent repair obligations, and a tribunal can order reimbursement if the provider doesn't repay the cost of urgent repairs within 7 days of written notice [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents do not contain the full notice procedure for 2019.
3. **Ask for lower rent:** The documents I retrieved do not contain a provision allowing a rent reduction for these defects in 2019, so I can't confirm this option.

## What the documents don't cover

- The 2019 text of the rental minimum standards (section 65A) and the 2019 regulations. The regulation versions I retrieved are dated 2025 and 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- The required form and timing of a termination notice under section 91L, and any compensation rules for this situation.
- Whether you have entered possession, since the Act doesn't define the term in the retrieved text.

I'd recommend checking the 2019 regulations and a Consumer Affairs Victoria or tenants' advice service before you act.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Nothing in the retrieved documents bars a rental provider from changing how rent is paid, but the rules set requirements you can check before paying. The documents don't say whether a change from agent to owner-managed is lawful, and they don't cover bank-detail scams.

**Which law applies:** On 8 November 2022, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 101, in force from 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 002, in force from 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) were both in force. I've relied on those versions.

**What the law says**

- **Payment method:** The rental provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than your own bank fees), and must allow you to use Centrepay or another electronic funds transfer. You are entitled to a receipt confirming each rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changes to contact details:** The rental provider must notify you within 7 days if the agent's details change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The standard form also says both parties must immediately notify the other in writing if their contact details change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond:** The rental provider or agent must lodge your bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of receiving it. If you don't receive an RTBA receipt within 15 business days of paying, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check before paying the new account**

1. **Get the change in writing.** The regulations require notice of changed details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Ask for the owner's full name, address, phone number and email, and the new payment details, in writing.
2. **Verify the request independently.** Call the owner on a number you already have, or one you find independently, not one given in the new message. The documents don't address fraud, so this is general advice.
3. **Check the payment method is fee-free.** Ask whether the method has any fees beyond your own bank fees. The law requires at least one fee-free option and Centrepay or EFT availability [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Confirm your bond is held.** Since you paid the bond through the agent, check that it was lodged with the RTBA within 10 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If you have no receipt, contact the RTBA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep records.** Get a receipt for every rent payment, which you are entitled to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't say whether an owner can take over management from an agent mid-lease, how a change of rental provider affects your agreement, or what to do if the new account turns out to be fraudulent. For those questions, consult Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't settle either question. They don't say whether you must be home for the inspection, and they don't address whether the agent can charge $90 to rebook.

**What applies on 3 December 2025**

The versions in force on that date are the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Authorised Version No. 111, in force from 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 005), in force from 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The Act version 115 and Regulations version 009 are dated 2026, so I did not rely on them [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says about the smoke alarm check**

- The landlord must ensure any smoke alarm is correctly installed, in working condition, fitted with batteries, and tested at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Testing, repair or replacement of a mains-powered smoke alarm must be done by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- If a smoke alarm doesn't meet these requirements, the renter may request urgent repairs, and the landlord or agent must immediately arrange them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be there to let the inspector in?**

The Regulations say the rental provider may enter to do an inspection, but not more than once every 12 months, and that "the renter must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Nothing I retrieved says the renter must personally attend, so I can't confirm that you must be home. The entry rules in the Act (ss 85–88, covering entry, grounds, and notice requirements) were not in the results for the version in force on 3 December 2025. Older versions exist in the results, but I haven't relied on them because they are not the law on your date [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Can the agent charge the $90?**

The documents don't answer this. The Act's table of contents lists "Certain charges prohibited" (s 51) and "Certain application and rent payment fees prohibited" (s 51A), but the text of those sections wasn't retrieved [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I found nothing about a rebooking fee.

**What you can do or ask**

- Ask the agent which section of the Act or Regulations authorises the entry and the $90 fee. Write to them, since the law requires notice in writing.
- Ask whether this is the only inspection in the 12-month period. The Regulations limit inspections to once every 12 months [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- If the smoke alarm is not working, make a written urgent repair request, which the agent must act on immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- For the entry and fee rules, check consumer.vic.gov.au/renting, which the Regulations reference [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the Act as in force on 15 January 2026, the card fee is likely unlawful if it is charged for paying rent. The renter can insist on a fee-free method. Whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent matters in part, but the main prohibition applies to any person.

**What the law says**

- **Charges for electronic payment facilities are prohibited.** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge in relation to "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units. This is s 51(3)(b) in the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The text does not carve out agents or third parties, so it applies to the app company whichever party receives the fee. The documents don't define "electronic payment facility," so whether a card payment falls within it is a reading I'm inferring, not something the documents state.
- **Agents must offer a fee-free method.** A provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter." The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Bank transfer appears to be this kind of method, since the regulations prescribe electronic funds transfer as a payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say how fast a method must be to count as "reasonably available," so the slower speed of bank transfer is not addressed.
- **Costs must be disclosed before consent.** The provider or agent must tell the renter about costs, "including third party transaction fees," that the renter may incur by using a particular payment method, before the renter consents to that method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent-payment fees (not yet in force).** Section 51A bars non-exempt businesses from charging fees for prescribed matters, including "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)." Agents are exempt from s 51A, but the payments company is not listed as exempt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the list of prescribed matters in Regulation 21C only takes effect on 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So as of 15 January 2026, the documents do not show a prescribed rent-payment fee ban in force. The documents also don't identify any "other Act" that permits payment surcharges.

**What the renter can do or ask**

1. **Ask the agent for the cost details** of card payment, including any third-party transaction fee, before agreeing to pay by card [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for a fee-free method.** Bank transfer (EFT) is a fee-free option you can request, and the agent must make a no-extra-cost method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask about Centrepay.** Providers must permit Centrepay as a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for a receipt.** If you request one at the time of payment, a written receipt must be given within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Raise the card fee directly.** You can tell the agent that you are not willing to pay the app's card fee, given the s 51(3)(b) prohibition.

**Other points**

- The documents don't say where or how to complain about the fee, so I can't advise on that.
- Your rent agreement may set out the permitted payment methods. Section 42(2) says rent is payable in the manner specified in the agreement, subject to the rest of s 42 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The documents also include later versions of the Act and Regulations. Those are not in force on 15 January 2026, so I have not relied on them.

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For a firm answer, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Under the Act version in force on 15 October 2019, the retrieved documents support only part of your question. - "Urgent repairs" include any fault or damage that makes rented premises "unsafe or insecure", including "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

- The definition of "renter" includes a person to whom premises are to be let under a proposed residential rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpts do not say whether repair duties apply before you move in.

**Your options**

- **Cancel:** The retrieved documents do not contain any provision on ending a lease before occupation, so I cannot say whether you can cancel or on what grounds.
- **Ask for repairs:** The damp and mould you describe match the urgent-repairs wording above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). - The content of the rental minimum standards (section 65A).
- The text of sections 60 and 67.
- The 2019 Residential Tenancies Regulations. The Regulations I retrieved (condition report form, repair rules) are from 2021 or later and are not in force on 15 October 2019, so I have not applied them.

For a firm answer, you would need the full Act at Version 088 and the regulations in force in October 2019. A lawyer, Consumer Affairs Victoria, or VCAT could also advise you. Those sources are outside the documents I searched.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**What the law says**

- **Change of agent or contact details:** The standard agreement form says the rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the rental provider's or agent's details change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It also says both parties must immediately notify the other in writing if their contact details change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Payment methods and receipts:** The rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees), and must allow the renter to use Centrepay or another electronic funds transfer. The renter is entitled to a receipt confirming payment of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond:** The rental provider holds bond on trust for the renter until it is paid to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider must give the bond to the RTBA within 10 business days after receiving it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The RTBA must send a receipt within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days after paying the bond, you may notify the RTBA [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**Which versions apply on 8 November 2022**

- Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002, in force from 1 June 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101, in force from 7 September 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can check or ask before paying**

1. **Get the change in writing and confirm the new details.** Ask for the owner's full name, address, phone and email, and check them against your agreement. The rental provider must give notice of changes to these details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Confirm the payment method.** Make sure the new account is a fee-free option and that you can get a receipt for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Check your bond.** Your bond should have gone to the RTBA, not to the agent or owner. Ask for the RTBA receipt. If you haven't received one within 15 business days of paying, you can contact the RTBA at rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or 1300 137 164 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Check that the agreement itself is still valid.** The documents I retrieved don't say whether an owner taking over management changes the agreement or requires a new one.

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether the owner can change the rent account partway through a tenancy without your agreement, beyond the notice requirements above.
- Whether an owner who takes over from an agent must sign a new agreement.
- Anything about how to verify bank details or prevent payment fraud.

For the last point, a common precaution is to confirm the new details by phoning the owner or agent on a number you already have, not one from the message. This is general advice, not from the documents. Also check your signed agreement, since its payment-details section may set out additional terms.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't settle either question. They don't say whether you must be present for a smoke alarm check, and they don't mention a $90 rebooking fee.

**Version in force on 3 December 2025:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 111, in force from 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 005, in force from 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says about smoke alarms**

- The landlord must ensure any smoke alarm is correctly installed, in working condition, fitted with batteries, and "tested at least once every 12 months in accordance with any instructions by the manufacturer of the smoke alarm" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Testing, repair or replacement of a mains-powered smoke alarm "must be undertaken by a suitably qualified person" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The regulations say the renter "must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- **Whether you must be home:** The current entry provisions (sections 85 to 89 of the Act) are not in the retrieved text of Version 111, so I can't tell you what notice or presence rules apply to an agent entering with a key.
- **Whether the $90 fee is allowed:** Nothing I retrieved addresses fees for inspections or rebooking. The only fee provisions I found concern consent to assignment or sub-letting, which isn't relevant here.
- **The 10 am to 12:30 pm weekday window:** I found no current rule on this.

I also found an older Act version (Version 098, in force 2021) with entry rules, including notice requirements and entry between 8 am and 6 pm [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf). It is no longer in force, so I can't rely on it for your situation.

**What you can do**

1. **Ask the agent in writing** what legal basis they're relying on, and whether you need to be present or can provide access another way. Your notice should state why they wish to enter; the 2021 version required this, but I can't confirm the current wording.
2. **Ask for the fee's legal basis** in writing. Nothing in the documents I reviewed supports a rebooking fee.
3. **Ask for a different time** if the window doesn't suit you. The documents don't say whether the agent must accommodate this.
4. **If a smoke alarm is faulty,** notify the landlord or agent in writing. The landlord or agent must "immediately arrange for the repairs to be carried out" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Contact Consumer Affairs Victoria** at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for guidance. The regulations refer readers to this site for rights information [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). For disputes about entry, VCAT is the tribunal, though the current version's entry provisions aren't in the documents I reviewed.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least not for a card fee charged on rent. The Act restricts fees for electronic rent payments, and the rule applies to whoever receives the fee, not just the agent. The documents don't say what counts as a "prescribed" fee, so check that point before relying on this.

The law in force on 15 January 2026 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 111, which applies from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 005, also applies on that date, until 9 February 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **No charge for electronic payment facilities.** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge, or an indemnity for a charge, relating to "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card payment is very likely an "electronic payment facility," so this is the most direct provision.
- **Fees for rent payment.** A business other than a rental provider, the provider's agent, or a deposit-taking institution must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The app company is not one of the excluded parties, so this rule may also apply to it.
- **Fee-free method must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs is reasonably available to the renter. The only costs allowed are bank or account fees on the renter's own bank account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Information before you choose.** The provider or agent must tell the renter about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, before the renter consents to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### Does it matter who gets the fee?

Not much, based on these provisions:

- The "no charge for electronic payment facilities" rule applies to any "person," so it covers the app company even though it isn't the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The fee-free method rule and the cost-disclosure rule bind the provider and agent. If the agent takes the fee, or lets the app run the payment with a fee, the agent is responsible for making a fee-free method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The fee-prohibition rule for rent payments excludes providers and agents, so an agent receiving the fee is less clearly caught by that particular section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the electronic payment facility rule still applies to "a person," so it is not a clear way out for the agent.

### What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent** in writing whether the card fee is charged by the app or the payment company, and what it is. The agent must have told you about these costs before you chose the card method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Use the bank transfer** if it is a fee-free method. Note that the Act requires a fee-free method to be "reasonably available," not that it be instant, so slowness alone does not make it unreasonable. The documents don't say how slow is too slow [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the agreement.** Rent is payable in the manner specified in the agreement, and the Regulations' standard terms refer to the provider's "preferred methods of payment" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). If the agreement names only card payment, ask the agent how to pay without the fee.
- **Keep records** of your payments and any fees charged. Receipts are required for rent payments, and you can request them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### Gaps in the documents

- The Act refers to a "prescribed matter" for fees, and to "prescribed" payment methods, but the retrieved text does not list them. I can't confirm whether a card surcharge is a prescribed fee under the Regulations.
- The retrieved documents don't cover how or where to complain, or what remedies are available.
- This is general information, not legal advice. If the fee is significant, consider speaking to a tenancy advice service.

answer:

**Governing version:** On 15 October 2019, the applicable law is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), Authorised Version No. 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I did not apply later versions, such as the one from 4 December 2019 [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 I retrieved [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) are not the version for that date, so I haven't relied on them.

### What the law says

- **Condition on move-in day:** The landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the day the tenant is due to move in. The retrieved text of v088 shows that a tenant is not required to enter premises that do not comply, and no rent is payable from the agreed day until the tenant actually moves in [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The full wording of that opening duty is only shown in a later version [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf), so I can't confirm its exact wording in v088.
- **Repairs:** The landlord must ensure rented premises are maintained in good repair [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Repairs must also leave premises in a "reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp:** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure", including "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Rotting timber could fall within the "unsafe or insecure" limb, but that depends on the facts.
- **Breach of duty:** Section 65 falls within the duties that can be enforced through a breach of duty notice [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The notice must specify the breach, give details of the loss, and require the landlord to remedy the breach or compensate you within the required time, which is 14 days for these duties [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

1. **Decline to move in:** Under the v088 text, you are not required to enter occupation of premises that do not comply, and you owe no rent for the period until you actually move in [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Cancel:** The retrieved v088 text does not show a right to terminate the lease for these defects. I can't confirm whether you can cancel, so you should check the lease and get advice on that point.
3. **Ask for repairs:**
   - Give written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - **Urgent repairs:** If you take reasonable steps to get the landlord to act immediately and they don't, you may arrange urgent repairs. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1,000, whichever is less [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can also apply to the Tribunal for an urgent repair order, which must be heard within 2 business days [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - **Non-urgent repairs:** You can apply to the Director to investigate if repairs aren't carried out within 14 days of written notice [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can then apply to the Tribunal, which must hear the application within 7 days [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - You can also give a breach of duty notice and then apply to the Tribunal for compensation or a compliance order [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - The retrieved text of these repair sections refers to a "tenant" or "renter" under a tenancy. It does not say whether they apply before you have moved in, so that point needs checking.
4. **Ask for lower rent or compensation:**
   - The Tribunal may order compensation that takes the form of a refund or reduction of rent [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - In deciding compensation, the Tribunal may consider whether you received any rent reduction or refund and whether you took steps to reduce your loss [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - You may apply to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if you have given a repair notice and the landlord has failed to carry out the repairs [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not say whether that applies before you move in.

---

**Gaps:** The documents don't cover a right to terminate the lease for these defects in v088, or how the repair provisions apply before a tenant moves in. This isn't legal advice. Consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT for advice on your specific lease.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't include the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* text in force on 8 November 2022, so I can't confirm the Act's rent-payment rules as they stood then. The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 002, in force 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024) does cover that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), and the Act provisions I describe below come from later versions.

**What the law says**

- **Payment methods:** The standard rental agreement form says the rental provider "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method and must allow the renter to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** "The renter is entitled to receive a receipt from the rental provider confirming payment of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing details:** The form says the rental provider "must notify the renter within 7 days if any of this information changes," which covers agent details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It also says the parties "must immediately notify the other party in writing if their contact details change" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond:** The rental provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days. If the renter has no receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, they may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing payment method (later Act):** The current Act (version 111, in force from 25 November 2025) says rent is payable "in the manner (if any) specified in the agreement," and that the provider and renter "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Version 110 (in force 6 August to 24 November 2025) has the same wording [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm this applied in 2022.
- **Costs and receipts (later Act):** The provider's agent must give the renter information about any costs, such as third-party transaction fees, that the renter may incur by using a payment method before the renter consents to it [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A written receipt must be signed by the person receiving payment and must state the renter's name and the rented premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What to check or ask before paying the new account**

1. **Ask for written confirmation** that the owner is now managing the property and that the agent is no longer acting. Under the form, the change must be notified to you in writing within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the change is agreed.** Under the later Act, a change in payment method is by agreement [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Don't treat an agent's email alone as agreement to change your payment arrangement.
3. **Confirm the account is fee-free for you** (apart from your own bank fees), and ask whether any costs apply before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Confirm the bond was lodged** with the RTBA and check whether you have a receipt. Because you paid a week ago, the 15-business-day window may not have passed yet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Get a receipt for each rent payment** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
6. **Verify the bank details independently.** The documents don't address how to verify a payee, so I can't advise on that from them. As a general precaution, confirm the new details through a contact you already have, not only the email that sent them.

**What the documents don't cover**

- The text of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in force on 8 November 2022.
- Whether the owner must give notice or go through any process to take over management.
- Whether the bank-detail change needed your written consent under the 2022 law.

You may want to check the Act version that applied in November 2022 directly, or ask a tenancy advice service such as Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: No. The bond point is covered ('Confirm the bond was lodged with the RTBA and check whether you have a receipt'). The agreement and known-contact point is also covered ('Don't treat an agent's email alone as agreement' and 'confirm the new details through a contact you already have'). The first point is incomplete: the answer says only that the provider 'must notify the renter within 7 days if any of this information changes' without saying what that information is. It never states that the landlord (the owner now managing) must give written notice of their full name, address for service and an emergency repairs number.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter can withhold rent, and it requires notice and written confirmation for the change, saying the change "must be notified to you in writing within 7 days" and that a change in payment method "is by agreement."

version-cited.reason: No — the answer never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Authorised Version No. 101 that was in force on 8 November 2022. Instead it relies on 'version 111, in force from 25 November 2025' and 'Version 110' for rules it presents as steps for the user, including that 'a change in payment method is by agreement' and the requirement to disclose costs before consent. These steps would change if the later-version material were deleted, so they count as reliance despite the caveat.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
## What the law says

On **Wednesday 3 December 2025**, the applicable documents are:

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* — **Authorised Version 111**, in force from 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* — **Authorised Version 005**, in force from 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The rental provider must ensure smoke alarms are working, have batteries, and are tested at least once every 12 months; mains-powered alarms must be tested, repaired or replaced by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

An agent may enter to enable the rental provider to perform a duty under the Act, including this smoke-alarm duty. For that purpose, at least **24 hours’ notice** is required, and entry must be between **8 am and 6 pm on a day other than a public holiday**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Your written notice seven days ahead for a weekday from 10 am to 12:30 pm therefore meets those timing requirements, assuming it also stated the reason and was delivered by post or personally. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

You must permit a person exercising that right of entry in accordance with the Act to enter. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) **The retrieved documents do not say that you personally must be home or that you must let the inspector in yourself.** They allow entry by the rental provider or the provider’s agent; they do not impose a personal-attendance requirement on the renter. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

**The retrieved documents do not contain any provision authorising a $90 rebooking fee for a smoke-alarm inspection, nor do they state whether such a fee may be charged.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Tell the agent in writing that:

1. you will permit lawful entry at the notified time;  
2. the agent may use its key and you will not personally attend; and  
3. they should identify the legal basis for the proposed **$90 fee**, because the retrieved documents do not address or authorise that fee. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

You can also ask the agent to confirm that the inspector is suitably qualified if the smoke alarm is mains-powered. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. For the hardest one, the answer says 'they do not impose a personal-attendance requirement on the renter' and advises telling the agent 'the agent may use its key and you will not personally attend'. It also states that the rental provider has the smoke-alarm testing duty and that entry needs 'at least 24 hours' notice' between '8 am and 6 pm', which the seven days' written notice meets.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither failing claim is made, since the answer says 'The retrieved documents do not say that you personally must be home or that you must let the inspector in yourself' and 'The retrieved documents do not contain any provision authorising a $90 rebooking fee', telling the renter to ask the agent for the fee's legal basis rather than to pay it.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with the in-force versions, the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025' (link 97-109aa111) and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025' (link 21-3sra005), and it relies on no other version for any rule it applies.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 January 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111**, in force from **25 November 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent **must ensure that a rent-payment method with no additional cost**—apart from fees charged to the renter’s own bank account—is **reasonably available**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Before the renter agrees to use a payment method, the rental provider or agent must disclose costs that may arise, including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- A person must not charge a renter for the **establishment or use of direct-debit facilities or another electronic payment facility** for paying rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, the existence of a fee-free manual bank-transfer option is important. If that option is reasonably available, the renter should not be required to pay the card fee to pay rent. The documents do not say whether being slower makes the transfer option unreasonable, so they do not establish that fact either way. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The documents also do **not clearly answer** whether the app company may voluntarily charge a card fee when the renter chooses the card option. They do, however, expressly refer to possible third-party transaction fees and require those costs to be disclosed beforehand. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

It does not necessarily matter that the fee is paid to the app company rather than the agent: the Act’s no-cost-method duty applies to the **rental provider or the provider’s agent**, while the prohibition on charging for the use of an electronic payment facility applies to **“a person.”** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not provide enough detail to determine conclusively whether this particular card surcharge is prohibited under that provision.

## What the renter can do or ask

Ask the agent, in writing:

1. To confirm that the manual bank-transfer method is available without any additional fee. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. Whether using the card option is optional and whether rent can be paid by bank transfer without disadvantage or penalty. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
3. For the amount and legal basis of the card fee, and when that fee was disclosed before consent to the payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
4. Whether the agent or rental provider receives any part of the fee, and whether the app company is charging it as a third-party transaction fee. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

If the transfer method is not reasonably available, or if the card fee is being required rather than merely charged for an optional method, the renter can raise that with the agent and seek advice or dispute resolution. The retrieved documents do not specify the exact complaint or tribunal procedure for this issue.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the first point ("must ensure that a rent-payment method with no additional cost... is reasonably available") but misses the second: it never says the specific ban on rent-payment fees (reg 21C) is not yet in effect on 15 January 2026 and only applies from 31 March 2026, and instead presents a prohibition as already applying.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never claims the card fee is already banned, saying instead that "The retrieved documents do not provide enough detail to determine conclusively whether this particular card surcharge is prohibited," and it affirms that a fee-free method is required: "The rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with no additional cost... is reasonably available."

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names the Act as "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111" (link 97-109aa111) but never mentions the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005, which is a required document in the first list.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019**—therefore the version in force on **15 October 2019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider must ensure that the premises are **vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day**. You are **not required to enter into occupation** if they do not meet that requirement, and you are **not required to pay rent from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually enter into occupation**. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must maintain the premises **in good repair**. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- Mould or damp **caused by or related to the building structure** is included in the Act’s definition of an **urgent repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- The Act does **not**, in the retrieved provisions, state an automatic right to cancel or rescind a signed lease merely because defects are discovered before moving in. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Do not move in until the condition is addressed.** Give the rental provider or agent written notice immediately, describing the damp, mould and rotting timber. Keep dated photographs, videos and copies of all communications. The Act requires notice of damage to be given as soon as practicable. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** If the mould or damp is structurally caused, or the rotting timber makes the property unsafe, ask the provider to arrange immediate repairs. If you cannot get the provider or agent to act, the Act permits a renter to arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to have the provider do them. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Seek an order for repairs.** For non-urgent repairs, give written notice. If the provider has not completed them within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director to investigate and may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For urgent repairs, you may apply to the Tribunal if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs exceed the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask for a rent adjustment, but do not assume you can impose one.** The retrieved provisions do not give you a general right simply to reduce the rent because the premises are defective. You may ask the provider to agree to a lower rent, but the statutory remedy described is an order for repairs and potentially compensation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Do not stop paying rent without an agreement or Tribunal order; instead, after giving repair notice, you may apply for an order allowing rent to be paid into the **Rent Special Account** while repairs remain outstanding. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Ask the provider to agree in writing to end the lease and refund any bond or rent paid.** The retrieved documents do not say that the provider must agree, nor do they set out a specific pre-occupation cancellation procedure. question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **8 November 2022**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002 (in force from 1 June 2022)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The prescribed rental agreement must state the rental provider’s details and, if an agent acts for them, the agent’s details. The rental provider must notify the renter **within 7 days** if any of that information changes. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The agreement must also state the rent-payment methods and payment details. The rental provider must permit at least one **fee-free payment method** (apart from the renter’s own bank fees) and must allow **Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer**. The renter is entitled to a receipt for rent paid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** say how a renter must authenticate changed bank details, or specifically explain the legal process when an agency stops managing the property.

## What you can do or ask

Before paying the new account, ask for written confirmation of:

- the owner’s full name and contact details;
- that the agency’s appointment has ended and the owner is now managing the tenancy;
- the effective date of the change; and
- the new rent-payment details, consistently with the payment details in the rental agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

You can also ask the owner or former agent to confirm the change through contact details already recorded in your signed agreement, rather than relying only on the new bank details. **The retrieved document does not expressly require this verification step**, so this is a precaution rather than a stated statutory requirement.

Keep proof of the request and any payment. Ask for a receipt, which you are entitled to receive. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

For the bond, check that it has been lodged with the **Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA)**. The rental provider or agent must lodge it within **10 business days** after receiving it; the RTBA should send you a receipt, and if you have not received one within **15 business days**, you may email **rtba@justice.vic.gov.au** or call **1300 137 164**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The answer does cover confirming through contact details already in the agreement and the RTBA bond receipt, but the first point is only partly covered: it mentions 'rental provider's details' and the 7-day change notice, not the address for service or the emergency repairs number.

My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?

## What the law says

On **3 December 2025**, the relevant documents were:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111**, in force from 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must ensure that smoke alarms are correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries, and tested at least every 12 months according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Mains-powered smoke-alarm testing must be done by a suitably qualified person. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The documents also **do not contain any provision authorising a $90 rebooking fee** for a smoke-alarm check, or otherwise say that this amount may be charged to the renter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can tell the agent in writing that:

1. You will allow the smoke-alarm inspection, but you are asking them to confirm the legal basis for requiring you to be personally present when they hold a key; and  
2. You dispute the **$90 fee** unless they identify a specific lawful basis for charging it.

The documents do not provide enough information to conclude whether the seven-day notice and the proposed weekday time satisfy every entry-procedure requirement.
