question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says — 15 January 2026

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 111**, dated **25 November 2025**, in force on 15 January 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version 005**, dated **25 November 2025**, also in force on that date. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**—apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account—is reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) A bank-transfer option with no fee appears to satisfy that requirement, even if it is slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

However, the Act also says that **“a person” must not demand or receive a charge or indemnity for a charge relating to the establishment or use of direct-debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) A card-payment fee charged by the app company may fall within that prohibition, but the retrieved documents do not expressly decide whether a particular card surcharge is such a prohibited charge. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The Act expressly requires information about costs—including **third-party transaction fees** and other electronic-payment-facility fees—before the renter consents to use a payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) That disclosure requirement does not, by itself, establish that every disclosed fee is lawful. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The newer provision prohibiting prescribed rent-payment fees does not resolve the position on 15 January 2026: the regulation prescribing **“rent payment”** as a prohibited matter expressly takes effect only on **31 March 2026**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents therefore do not establish that this later prohibition was already in force on 15 January.

**Does it matter who receives the fee?** The wording of the existing electronic-payment-facility prohibition applies to **“a person”**, not only to the rental provider or agent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Accordingly, the fact that the fee goes to the payments company rather than the agent does not automatically make it lawful. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) But the documents do not provide a definitive classification of this particular app’s card fee.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or payments company:

1. **What is the legal basis for the card fee?**
2. **Who demands and receives it?**
3. **Why is it charged when a fee-free bank-transfer method is available?**
4. **Was the fee and its amount disclosed before you consented to use the card-payment method?** The Act requires information about applicable payment-method costs before consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

You can also state that you wish to use the **fee-free bank-transfer option**, which the rental provider or agent must make reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) If they insist that the card fee is payable, the retrieved documents do not provide enough information to give a conclusive answer about this particular surcharge; they do establish that the recipient being the app company, rather than the agent, is not by itself decisive. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says a no-extra-cost method must be reasonably available and that 'A bank-transfer option with no fee appears to satisfy that requirement, even if it is slower.' It also says the regulation prescribing 'rent payment' as a prohibited matter 'expressly takes effect only on 31 March 2026', so a reader can tell that fee ban is not yet in force on 15 January.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not claim the card fee is already banned under the newer rent-payment fee prohibition; it says the regulation prescribing "rent payment" "expressly takes effect only on 31 March 2026" and that the documents "do not establish that this later prohibition was already in force on 15 January." It also affirms, rather than denies, a fee-free rule: the provider or agent "must ensure that a rent-payment method with no additional cost... is reasonably available."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version 111, dated 25 November 2025' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 — Authorised Version 005, dated 25 November 2025'; every rule it applies comes from those versions (links 97-109aa111 and 21-3sra005), and it mentions the 31 March 2026 rent-payment regulation only to say it is not yet in effect.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law said on 15 October 2019

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088**, incorporating amendments as at **2 July 2019**. It was in force on 15 October 2019. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord had to provide premises that were **vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day**. You were **not required to enter into occupation** if they did not meet that requirement. If they did not, you were **not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually entered into occupation**. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had to maintain the premises in **good repair**. This duty applied even if you knew about the disrepair before entering into occupation, and regardless of the rent, age or character of the premises. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure was listed as an **urgent repair** where it made the premises unsafe or insecure. [[15]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not specifically classify rotting timber as an urgent repair, although it may support an argument that the premises are not in good repair or are unsafe. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to cancel the agreement by mutual agreement.** The documents do not give you an automatic right to cancel merely because you discovered damp, mould and rotting timber before moving in. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Give written notice requiring repairs.** For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord does not repair them within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director to investigate and then potentially to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) If the mould or damp is an urgent repair, you can require immediate action; if the landlord does not act, the Act allowed you to arrange the urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them, subject to the statutory procedure. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Do not move in while the problem remains**, if the premises do not meet the statutory requirements. You are not required to enter into occupation, and you do not have to pay rent for the period before you actually enter into occupation if the premises do not comply with section 65. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask for a rent reduction**, but it would need to be agreed with the landlord; the documents do not provide a general right to impose a lower rent before moving in. If repairs are not done, you may instead apply to the Tribunal for permission to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account**. [[13]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **If the premises are unfit for human habitation**, you may give a notice of intention to vacate specifying termination on the day of the notice or a later date. Whether the conditions you describe meet that legal threshold is not determined by the documents. [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa097%20authorised.pdf)

Preserve photographs, inspection reports and written communications, and write to the landlord or agent immediately describing each defect and stating that you have not entered into occupation.

must-mention.reason: No: the first required point is missing and is contradicted. The answer says 'The documents do not give you an automatic right to cancel merely because you discovered damp, mould and rotting timber before moving in' and offers only cancellation by mutual agreement. It never states that a renter who has not moved in can end the agreement by notice under s 226 because the premises are not in good repair. Its only reference to termination for unfitness for habitation is hedged and cites a 2021 version of the Act. The repairs point (s 68 good repair, urgent repairs for mould or damp) and the evidence point (photographs and inspection reports) are covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the rental minimum standards or a mould and damp standard applied. It treats mould and damp only as an 'urgent repair' under the 1997 Act and the landlord's duty of 'good repair'. It also does not say the renter must move in, stating instead 'You were not required to enter into occupation' and 'Do not move in while the problem remains'.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088... as at 2 July 2019', but it applies two rules that were not in force on 15 October 2019. First, it treats 'mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure' as an urgent repair and builds a repair step on that, yet this comes only from the not-yet-commenced 2018 amendments. Second, its unfit-for-habitation notice to vacate is sourced from version 097 (97-109aa097), which was not the version in force on that date.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
## What the law says

On **3 December 2025**, the applicable versions are:

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 111**, in force from **25 November 2025**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Entry is permitted when needed for the rental provider to carry out a duty under the Act. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

For that type of entry, the Act requires entry between **8 am and 6 pm**, on a day other than a public holiday, with at least **48 hours’ notice**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf) A notice must be in writing, state the reason for entry, and be given by post or personally between **8 am and 6 pm**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)

You must permit a person exercising a valid right of entry to enter. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do **not** say that the renter must personally be home to let the person in. Therefore, if the agent can lawfully provide access using its key, the documents do not establish any requirement for you to be present.

The retrieved documents do **not** contain a rule authorising or prohibiting a **$90 rebooking fee**. I therefore cannot say from these documents that the agent can charge it.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?

- A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge connected with the **establishment or use of an electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The documents do not expressly address a payments company’s contractual relationship with the agent, but they do not provide an exception for third-party app operators. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord had to provide the premises **vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day**. You were **not required to enter into occupation** if they did not comply. You were also **not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually entered into occupation**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had a continuing duty to maintain the premises **in good repair**. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure was expressly included in the Act’s definition of **urgent repairs**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Do not move in until the condition is dealt with.** The Act says you do not have to enter into occupation if the premises do not meet the statutory requirement. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Give the landlord or agent written notice immediately.** Describe and photograph the damp, mould and rotting timber, and state that you require the premises to be made safe and repaired. The landlord’s duty is to maintain the premises in good repair. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask for urgent repairs.** Structural damp or mould may fall within the urgent-repairs definition. If the landlord cannot be contacted or will not arrange the repairs immediately, you may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to contact them; the landlord’s reimbursement liability was limited to the reasonable cost or **$1,000, whichever was less**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)  
   If you cannot meet the cost, the repairs cost more than **$1,000**, or the landlord refuses to pay, you could apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the urgent repairs. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **For non-urgent repairs**, you could give written notice and, if the landlord did not repair within **14 days**, apply to the Director for an investigation. After receiving the Director’s report, you could apply to the Tribunal for a repairs order; the application generally had to be made within **60 days** of receiving the report. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Ask to cancel the lease by agreement.** The retrieved provisions do **not** state that a renter has an automatic right to cancel solely because defects are discovered before moving in. They also do not provide a specific cancellation procedure on these facts. Therefore, obtain the landlord’s written agreement releasing you from the lease and confirming any refund of rent or bond.

6. **Ask for lower rent.** You can ask the landlord to agree to a rent reduction, but the retrieved provisions do **not** establish an automatic right to reduced rent merely because you have not yet moved in. They do establish that no rent is payable for the period beginning on the agreed occupation day and ending when you actually enter occupation if the premises fail the statutory condition. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Keep paying nothing that the Act says is not payable, but do not simply treat the lease as cancelled without written agreement or a Tribunal order. The documents do not contain enough information to say that handing over the keys, without moving in or staying there, by itself terminated the agreement.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:

On **8 November 2022**, the applicable documents were:

The prescribed rental agreement identifies both the **rental provider** and, if applicable, the **rental provider’s agent**, including their names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses. The rental provider must notify you **within 7 days if any of that information changes**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The agreement must also state the available rent-payment methods and payment details. You are entitled to a receipt confirming rent paid, and the rental provider must allow at least one fee-free payment method, as well as Centrepay or another electronic-funds-transfer method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** specifically state the procedure for changing from an agency-managed tenancy to owner management, or for changing the bank account into which rent is paid. They therefore do not establish, by themselves, that the new bank details are genuine.

## What you can do or ask

Before paying the new account, ask for:

1. **Written confirmation of the management change**, identifying the owner as the rental provider and confirming that the agency no longer receives rent.
2. **Updated rental-provider and agent details**, if the details in your signed agreement have changed; the change should be notified within 7 days. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. **Written confirmation of the new rent-payment details**, including the account name, BSB, account number and the date from which they apply, and a receipt for your payment. The payment details should correspond with the agreement or a written update to it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
4. **Confirmation that your bond has been lodged with the RTBA.** The rental provider or agent must complete and give you a bond lodgment form when the bond is paid, lodge the bond with the RTBA within **10 business days**, and the RTBA must issue you a receipt. If you have not received the RTBA receipt within **15 business days**, you may notify the Authority. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

Until you have verified the change through a reliable existing contact for the agency or owner, you can ask the agent to confirm the instruction in writing rather than relying only on the message containing the new bank details. The retrieved documents do not prescribe a particular verification method.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?

There is no legal requirement for you to be physically present to let the inspector in. As long as the agent provided the required written notice and followed the correct entry procedures, they are entitled to use their key to grant access.

No. The retrieved regulations do not authorize any fees for rebooking inspections or smoke alarm checks [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Furthermore, testing smoke alarms is a statutory duty of the rental provider, who `"must ensure that any smoke alarm installed in rented premises is... tested at least once every 12 months"` [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Because complying with this safety obligation falls entirely on them, they cannot legally pass rebooking costs onto you. You can refuse to pay the $90 fee.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say you must be home, and they don't say the agent can charge a $90 rebooking fee. They also don't contain the entry-rights sections as they stood on 3 December 2025, so some of this is indicative only.

## Which version applies
On 3 December 2025 the Act in force was *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf* (version 111, in force from 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations in force were *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf* (version 005) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved extract of version 111 stops at around section 71. It does not include the entry provisions (ss 85–91A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The only text of those sections I found is in *rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf* (version 101, dated 7 September 2022) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). That is an earlier version, so treat what follows as a guide and not as the law in force on 3 December 2025.

## What the law says
- **Smoke alarm duty (version 111):** The rental provider must make sure each smoke alarm is working and has batteries. It must also be tested at least every 12 months. Testing a mains-powered alarm must be done by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry rights (version 101 text only):** The provider or agent may enter with the people needed for the purpose. For entry to carry out a duty under the Act, they need at least 24 hours' notice, and entry must be between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on a day that isn't a public holiday [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Your 7 days' notice and 10 am–12:30 pm window fit within that.
- **Notice form (version 101 text only):** The notice must be in writing, say why they want to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Check yours meets this.
- **Manner of entry (version 101 text only):** Entry must be in a reasonable manner. People must not stay longer than needed without your consent [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty (version 101 text only):** You must permit entry that follows these rules [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Regulations' standard-form summary also says you must allow entry where the rental provider has followed proper procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be there?** In the text I retrieved, your duty is to "permit" entry [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Nothing there says you must be present. Nothing there addresses an agent entering with a key while you are out either. I can't confirm from these documents whether either is allowed.

**Can they charge $90?** I found no provision about rebooking or missed-appointment fees. I tried two further searches on this and both failed, so this is a gap in what I could retrieve. It is not proof that no such rule exists.

## What you can do
- **Ask the agent in writing** what legal basis they rely on for requiring your presence and for the $90 fee. Ask them to confirm the entry would happen within the notice terms.
- **Check the notice** for the stated reason, written form, and delivery method [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Go to the Tribunal if needed.** Under the version 101 text, you can apply to the Tribunal to limit when entry may occur [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If an entry doesn't comply with the entry rules, you can apply for an order restraining further entry for a set period [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Entering without complying, without reasonable excuse, is an offence [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Contact Consumer Affairs Victoria** to confirm the current rules. The Regulations list their number as 1300 55 81 81 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The second point, on the landlord's smoke alarm duty and 24 hours' written notice between 8 am and 6 pm, is covered.

It presents these as the law and as steps the user can take, and deleting them would substantially change the answer, even with the caveat that they are only a guide.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't give a clear yes or no. The Act restricts fees on rent payments, but whether this card fee is caught depends on a point the retrieved text doesn't settle. I've applied the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* as at 15 January 2026. That is the version in force from 25 November 2025 to 2026-06-29, and its file name and metadata give it as version 111 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The extract doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." label, so "111" is taken from that metadata.

## What the law says

- **Free method required (s 42(4)).** The provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A free bank transfer option is relevant here. The Act doesn't say whether a slower free method counts as "reasonably available", so I can't say it clearly does or doesn't.
- **Electronic payment facility charges (s 51(3)(b)).** A "person" must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for paying rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This isn't limited to the agent. If a card payment through the app is an "electronic payment facility", the rule could cover the payments company. The documents don't say whether it does.
- **Business fees on rent payments (s 51A).** A person carrying on a business must not demand or receive a fee for any *prescribed matter* relating to the payment of rent. The exceptions are the rental provider, the provider's agent, and authorised deposit-taking institutions (banks and similar) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
  - The payments company is none of those, so it isn't exempt.
  - The ban only applies to "prescribed matters". The retrieved Regulations extract (*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 005, in force 25 November 2025 to 2026-02-09) doesn't list them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm whether a card fee is one.
- **Disclosure (s 42(7)).** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Standard form note.** The Regulations' form notes say the rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method, other than the renter's own bank fees [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

Yes, in part.
- Under s 51A, the agent and provider are exempt, but a separate payments company is not [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A fee going to the app company is therefore more exposed than one kept by the agent. That still depends on the "prescribed matter" point above.
- Section 51(3)(b) refers to "a person" and doesn't depend on who receives the fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The agent's own duties under s 42(4) and s 42(7) apply regardless of who collects the fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

A later version of the Act (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) substituted a different s 51A [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It wasn't in force on 15 January 2026, so I haven't relied on it.

## What you can do

1. **Use the free bank transfer.** It avoids the fee entirely, and your own bank's fees are the only cost the Act allows for a no-cost method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the agent in writing** to confirm the cost of each payment method, including third party fees, as s 42(7) requires before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Also ask them to confirm that a no-cost method is reasonably available to you, as s 42(4) requires [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Don't agree to the card fee** unless you're happy with it. The Act allows the payment method to be changed by agreement (s 42(6)), so it's your choice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the prescribed matters** in the current Regulations, or get advice, if you want to challenge the fee. The retrieved documents don't cover that or say where to complain.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer omits the point that the specific rent-payment fee ban is not yet in effect on 15 January 2026 (reg 21C applies from 31 March 2026); it only says the retrieved Regulations don't list the prescribed matters, and it suggests the s 51A ban may already catch the payments company's fee.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the fee is already banned under s 51A or reg 21C; it says "I can't confirm whether a card fee is one" of the prescribed matters. It also affirms the fee-free rule: "The provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs... is reasonably available to you" (s 42(4)).

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 111" (link 97-109aa111) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 005" (link 21-3sra005). It mentions version 115 only to say it was not in force on 15 January 2026 and was not relied on, so deleting it would not change the answer's substance.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## Which law applies

On 15 October 2019 the version in force was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088** (*rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, in force 2 July to 3 December 2019) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The extracts I retrieved from that version are endnote pages and don't include the operative text of the sections on handing over premises, repairs or rent. The operative text I found is in **Version 089** (*rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf*, in force from 4 December 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). That is **later than your date**. I can't confirm from the documents that the wording was identical on 15 October 2019, so treat what follows as indicative only.

## What the law says

- **Handing over the premises.** On the agreed day the landlord must make sure the premises are "vacant and in a reasonably clean condition" (s 65(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- **Not having to move in.** A tenant "is not required to enter into occupation of premises which do not comply" with that duty (s 65(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether damp, mould and rotting timber count as not being "reasonably clean". That is the key question for this section.
- **Rent.** If the premises don't comply, you don't pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually enter into occupation (s 65(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs.** The landlord must ensure the premises "are maintained in good repair" (s 68(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

**1. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs (s 72).** You can arrange them yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them immediately and couldn't. You must give 14 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, up to $1000 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal for urgent repairs (s 73).** You can apply if you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $1000, or the landlord refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs (s 74).** Give the landlord written notice. If the repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can apply in writing to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). Section 75 allows a Tribunal application, but my extract cuts off before the details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- **What counts as "urgent".** The retrieved text doesn't define it, so I can't say whether mould or rot qualifies.

**2. Ask for lower rent**
- Under s 65(3) you owe no rent for the period before you move in, if the premises don't comply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- Separately, the Tribunal must declare rent excessive if it is more than a tenant should reasonably pay, having regard to "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" (s 47(3)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order a refund of the difference (s 48) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). The start of s 47, including who can apply and when, is cut off in my extract.

**3. Cancel the lease**
- **Landlord's notice (Version 090).** The only termination provision for unfit premises that I found in a version close to your date lets the **landlord** give a notice to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" (s 245, Version 090, *rta-1997-v090-2020-03-02.pdf*, from 2 March 2020) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2020-02/97-109aa090%20authorised.pdf).
- **Tenant's notice.** A **renter's** right to give notice of intention to vacate for premises "unfit for human habitation" (s 91ZD) appears only in the amending text in the Version 088 endnotes [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). In that text the party is called a "renter" and the other party a "residential rental provider". The documents don't show that this was in force on 15 October 2019.
- **Result.** I can't say from these documents whether you can cancel on that basis, or what a tenant's termination right for this problem was at that date.

## Gaps

For a definite answer on cancelling, and on whether mould and rot fall within s 65, check the Version 088 operative text. The Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT guidance current at that date would also help. Those materials weren't in what I retrieved.

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing: the answer never says that a renter who has not moved in can end the agreement by notice because the premises are not in good repair or are unfit (s 226), and instead concludes 'I can't say from these documents whether you can cancel on that basis'. The answer also hedges on whether serious damage counts as urgent repairs. It frames the question as whether the premises are 'reasonably clean', not whether they are in disrepair or unfit.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither forbidden claim is made. The answer never says the premises must meet rental minimum standards or a mould and damp standard on 15 October 2019, and it says the s 91ZD 'renter' provision is not shown to be 'in force on 15 October 2019'. It also says the opposite of 'no choice but to move in and pay rent', stating a tenant 'is not required to enter into occupation of premises which do not comply' and 'you don't pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually enter into occupation'.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088' as the version in force, but every operative rule it applies, including s 65, s 68, ss 72-75 and ss 47-48, comes from the later 'Version 089 (rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf, in force from 4 December 2019)'. It presents these as the law and as steps the user can take, which counts as relying on a later version despite the 'indicative only' caveat.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Version applied:** On 8 November 2022 the version in force was the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf" (document dated 7 September 2022). Its metadata gives Version 101, in force from 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The text I retrieved does not print the words "Authorised Version No.", so I am taking the number from the file name and metadata. I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf" (1 June 2022), Version 002, in force until 30 November 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Where and how rent is paid:** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the premises if none is specified. It is payable in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The rental provider and renter may change how rent is paid only "by agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Check what your signed agreement says about payment details, because a change of account is a change to the agreed payment manner.
- **A fee-free option:** The provider or their agent must make a payment method with no extra costs available. Your own bank fees are not counted as extra costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Costs information:** Before you consent to a payment method, you must be given information about any costs, such as third-party transaction fees or direct debit dishonour fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** If you pay without handing over cash in person and ask for a receipt when you pay, the person who receives the rent must give you a written receipt within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed by the person receiving the payment. It must state your name and the premises, the date, the period covered, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If no receipt is required, the recipient must keep a record for 12 months. If you ask for a copy, they must give it to you within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changed contact details:** The standard rental agreement form says the rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the provider's or agent's details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This is a note in the prescribed form. It applies if your agreement is on that form (Form 1), and I can't tell that from your question.
- **Your bond:** If the agent is no longer involved, check the bond. Under Part 10, "residential rental provider" includes the provider's agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - The provider or agent must complete a bond lodgment form with you at the time you pay, and give you a copy once you sign it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - They must pay the bond to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - Until it is paid to the Authority, they hold it on trust for you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - The Authority must send you a receipt within 7 days of receiving the bond [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - If you have no Authority receipt within 15 business days of paying, you may notify the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The lease form gives the contact details as rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or 1300 13 71 64 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. Ask for the change in writing, with the owner's full name and contact details. Compare these with the details in your signed agreement.
2. Check your agreement's payment clause. If it specifies an account or method, you don't have to agree to a different one, though you may agree to a change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. Ask what costs, if any, the new payment method involves, and whether a fee-free option is available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. Ask for written receipts for each payment, and ask for them at the time you pay so the 5-business-day deadline applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. Check that you have your bond lodgment form copy. Look for the Authority's receipt, or ask the agent for the bond number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents do not set out any process for verifying that new bank details are genuine, and they do not say how a change of manager must be notified. Calling the agency on a number you already hold is a common-sense precaution. It does not come from these documents.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say a renter must be home to let the inspector in. They also don't authorise, or prohibit, a $90 rebooking fee. They do cover the notice and entry rules.

**Documents used (law in force on 3 December 2025)**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", version 111, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf", version 005, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The search also returned later versions (RTA v115 of 13 Oct 2026 and Regulations v009 of 30 Jun 2026). They post-date today, so I haven't relied on them.

## What the law says

- **Smoke alarms:** The rental provider must ensure smoke alarms are working, have batteries and are tested at least once every 12 months. Mains-powered alarms must be tested by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Right of entry:** The provider or agent may enter, with the people needed for the purpose, between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, after notice under section 88 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice period:** Entry to carry out a duty under the Act (s 86(1)(c)) needs at least 24 hours' notice. A smoke alarm check most plausibly falls here, because it is a provider duty. Seven days' notice applies to valuation and routine inspections (s 86(1)(d) and (f)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your seven days' notice would satisfy either.
- **Notice contents:** The notice must be in writing and say why they want to enter. It must be sent by post or handed to you personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty:** You must "permit" entry that is made in accordance with this Division [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' summary says the same: you must allow entry where the provider has followed proper procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner of entry:** Entry must be reasonable. They must not stay longer than needed without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Do you have to be there?

- The Act gives a right to *enter* within the notified window and a duty on you to *permit* it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The retrieved text doesn't say you must be present, and it doesn't say you can insist on being present. Nothing in it addresses an agent using their own key. So I can't say from these documents that your absence is a breach.

## Can they charge $90?

- Nothing in the retrieved provisions allows a fee for missing or rebooking an entry appointment.
- Nothing in them expressly prohibits one either. The only fee prohibition I found concerns fees for consenting to assignment or sub-letting, which doesn't apply here [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- So the documents don't answer this part. Check your rental agreement and the Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance.

## What you can do

- **Check the notice:** It should be in writing, state the purpose, and be posted or personally delivered between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Agree another time:** The agent can enter at any time you agree to, if you consent within the 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the Tribunal:** You can apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying or limiting the days and times of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **If they breach the entry rules:** You can apply to the Tribunal to restrain entry for a set period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entering without reasonable excuse outside the Division is an offence carrying 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On presence, the answer says 'The documents don't say a renter must be home to let the inspector in' and notes the renter's duty is to 'permit' entry, which the rubric accepts because a point that the law does not require something is met by saying the documents do not require it. On notice, it says smoke alarm testing is the provider's duty and that entry to carry out a duty 'needs at least 24 hours' notice', in writing, with entry between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., adding that 'Your seven days' notice would satisfy either.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must be home or must pay the fee; it states "The documents don't say a renter must be home to let the inspector in. They also don't authorise, or prohibit, a $90 rebooking fee."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 ... version 111' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 ... version 005', both in force on 3 December 2025, and every rule it applies cites links 97-109aa111 or 21-3sra005. It mentions RTA v115 and Regulations v009 only to say they post-date today and were not relied on.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Document used:** *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (version 111). Its metadata shows it was in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), so it covers 15 January 2026. The excerpts don't show a separate "Authorised Version number" label, so "111" is the version number in the metadata.

## What the law says

- **A fee-free method must be reasonably available.** Under s 42(4), the provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Bank fees or account fees on your own bank account don't count as additional costs. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Your free bank transfer probably meets that test.** The Act doesn't say whether a slower free method is still "reasonably available", so the documents don't settle that point [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **You must be told about costs first.** Under s 42(7), the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using a payment method before you consent to it. The Act lists "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" as examples [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **So on the text I retrieved, a card fee isn't banned outright.** It must be disclosed in advance, and the free option must stay reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **In s 42, no.** The excerpt doesn't distinguish between a fee kept by the agent and one kept by a third-party payments company. It expressly mentions third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Another section may matter more.** A later version, *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (in force from 13 Oct 2026, after your date), has these provisions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - **s 51(3)** says a person must not demand or receive a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent".
  - **s 51A** says a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter relating to the payment of rent. The amendment notes show it was substituted by No. 46/2025.
- **I can't confirm those apply on 15 January 2026.** The v111 excerpts I retrieved don't include ss 51 or 51A, so I can't say what they provided in January 2026. I also don't have the Regulations in force on that date, so I can't say what is "prescribed" for s 51A. Attributing them to v111 would be a guess.
- **Why this matters.** s 51(3) is worded as "a person" and mentions electronic payment facilities. If it applied in January 2026, it could cover a card fee whoever receives it, which may make the app's fee unlawful.

## What you can do

1. **Ask for written disclosure.** Ask the agent to confirm in writing the card fee and who receives it. You're entitled to this before you consent (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Use the free bank transfer.** The Act requires a no-extra-cost method to be reasonably available to you (s 42(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Say so if the free option isn't practical.** If the transfer is too slow or impractical for you, tell the agent. Whether that breaches s 42(4) isn't answered in these documents.
4. **Check ss 51(3) and 51A in the version in force in January 2026.** The documents I retrieved don't let me say whether they prohibit the card fee. This is the key open question.

The documents don't cover complaint or enforcement pathways, so I can't advise on those.

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is covered: the answer says a no-extra-cost method must be reasonably available under s 42(4) and that 'Your free bank transfer probably meets that test.' The second point is missing. The answer never says the rent-payment fee ban (reg 21C, from 31 March 2026) is not yet in effect on 15 January 2026. It only says 'I can't confirm those apply on 15 January 2026' and even suggests s 51(3) 'may make the app's fee unlawful,' which leaves the reader unable to tell which way it falls.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer does not say the fee is already banned, since it states "I can't confirm those apply on 15 January 2026" and "a card fee isn't banned outright", and it affirms that "a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you" is required under s 42(4).

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names the Act as "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf" (version 111) but never names the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 Authorised Version No. 005, saying only "I also don't have the Regulations in force on that date." It also relies on the later "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" for ss 51(3) and 51A, both in its "Why this matters" analysis and as a step for the user.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Document applied:** *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019. Its metadata shows it was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I have not used the later versions (v089 onwards). The v088 file also contains amending text from a later Act, but I relied only on the operative text, which still uses "landlord" and "tenant" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Condition on the move-in day.** On the agreed day you were to enter occupation, the landlord must ensure the premises are "vacant and in a reasonably clean condition" (s 65(1)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **You can decline to move in.** A tenant is not required to enter into occupation of premises that don't meet s 65(1) (s 65(2)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **No rent until you move in.** If the premises don't comply, you don't have to pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually enter occupation (s 65(3)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs.** The landlord must ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair (s 68(1)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Limit of s 65.** Section 65 speaks only of "vacant" and "reasonably clean". The retrieved text does not say whether damp, mould or rotting timber counts as not "reasonably clean". The rent and occupation protection in s 65 may therefore not clearly cover your problem. Section 68 (good repair) fits rotting timber better.

## What you can do

**1. Repairs**
- Give the landlord or agent written notice that repairs are needed. A tenant must also notify the landlord as soon as practicable of damage they become aware of (s 62) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If the landlord hasn't done the non-urgent repairs within 14 days, you can apply in writing to the Director to investigate (s 74) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can then apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. This must be within 60 days of receiving the Director's report (s 75(2)). If the Director hasn't reported within 90 days of your application, you can apply without the report (s 75(5)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If the Tribunal finds the landlord in breach of the duty to maintain, it may order specified repairs, with a deadline (s 76) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- For **urgent** repairs, you can arrange them yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to act immediately and couldn't. Give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and cost (s 72(2)(a)). The landlord is liable for the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less (s 72(2)(b)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than the limit, or the landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to the Tribunal, which must hear it within 2 business days (s 73) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- After giving repair notice, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord fails to carry out the repairs (s 77) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Lower rent**
- Section 65(3) relieves you of rent until you enter occupation, but only if the premises fail s 65(1) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Apart from that, the v088 text I retrieved has no general right to a rent reduction for defects. The nearest provisions are excessive-rent complaints to the Director, which apply where services or facilities were reduced or withdrawn, or where you've received a rent-increase notice (s 45) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For a Tribunal excessive-rent order, "the state of repair and general condition" is one factor (s 47(3)(b)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That path depends on a Director's report (s 46) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), and it doesn't clearly fit your situation.

**3. Cancelling**
- The retrieved v088 text has no provision on ending a lease before you take possession. Section 65(2) lets you refuse to enter occupation, but the text I found doesn't say it lets you end the agreement or get out of your obligations.
- I also did not find the Tribunal's compensation power (s 212) in the v088 text, so I can't say whether you can claim compensation.

**Next step:** on cancelling and compensation, the documents don't answer. Put your complaint in writing to the landlord or agent now, and get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service before deciding whether to walk away.

Instead it states 'The retrieved v088 text has no provision on ending a lease before you take possession.' It also does not tie the right to cancel to disrepair or unfitness rather than mere uncleanliness, though it does cover s 68 repairs and urgent repairs.

The answer names 'rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019', which was the version in force on 15 October 2019. It relies only on that version's operative provisions (ss 45–47, 62, 65, 68, 72–77, including the pre-2021 $1000 urgent-repair limit). It does not apply rules found only in the 'Amendments Not in Operation' section, such as the rental minimum standards or mould and damp as an urgent repair.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Before you pay, get the change confirmed in writing and check it with the agent you dealt with. The retrieved documents don't say how to verify bank details, so that part is practical caution and not law. The law below is the version in force on 8 November 2022.

## What the law says

- **Notice of change.** The standard rental agreement form (Form 1) in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* says the rental provider "must notify the renter within 7 days if any of this information changes". The information covers the rental provider's details and the agent's details: name, address, phone, ACN and email [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That document is rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf, Version 002, in force 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Act's own section 66(4) (7 days' written notice of a change) appears only in a later document, rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf (Version 115, 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act version in force on 8 November 2022 is rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf (Version 101, in force 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), and the retrieved text of it doesn't include section 66. I can't attribute section 66 to the 2022 Act.
- **Payment details.** The same form has a "Payment details" field and a list of payment methods the provider offers [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It says the provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (apart from your own bank fees) and must allow you to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts.** You are entitled to a receipt from the rental provider confirming payment of rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Contact changes.** The form says the provider and renter "must immediately notify the other party in writing if their contact details change" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Your bond.**
  - A provider who receives bond must give you a bond lodgment form to sign at payment, and a copy once you sign [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - They must pay the bond to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - For bonds, "residential rental provider" includes an agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - The bond is held on trust for you until it reaches the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - The Authority must send you a receipt within 7 days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - If you have no receipt within 15 business days of paying, you may notify the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Regulations say you can email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 13 71 64 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the change in writing**, signed or sent by the agency, and confirm it with the agent using contact details you already hold, not details in the new message. This is a precaution; the documents don't address verification or fraud.
2. **Ask for the owner's full name, address and contact details.** Form 1 expects these where no agent is acting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Check whether the agency still holds your bond.** Look for the bond lodgment form copy and the Authority's receipt. You paid about a week ago, so the 10-business-day lodgment window may still be open and the 15-business-day point hasn't been reached. If the bond hasn't been lodged, the agent may need to hand over the bond or the lodgment before the changeover. The documents don't say what happens to a bond when management changes hands, so I can't tell you more than that.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't say you must be home, and they don't say the agent can charge a $90 rebooking fee. The sections on entry are only in an older, superseded version of the Act, so I can't confirm the rules on 3 December 2025 from the documents.

## What the law says

**Which versions apply today (3 Dec 2025):**
- The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 111 (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf), is in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version 005 (rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf), is in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The later versions in the search results (Act v115 and Regulations v009, both dated 2026) were not in force today, so I haven't relied on them.

**What the in-force documents say:**
- The rental provider must ensure smoke alarms work, have batteries, and are tested at least once every 12 months (Act s 68AA) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The standard-form summary in the Regulations says the rental provider may enter "to comply with the rental provider's duties under the Act". It also says "the renter must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Neither document, in the parts retrieved, says whether you must be present when entry happens. Neither mentions a fee for rebooking or missing an appointment.

**The entry rules themselves:**
- The detailed entry sections (ss 85–89) did not appear in the retrieved text of Act v111 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- They appear only in an older version, *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf), dated 7 Sep 2022 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). That version is not the one in force today, and I can't tell from the documents whether the wording has changed since.
- That 2022 text says a notice of entry must be in writing, state why the agent wants to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. (s 88) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- It says a renter has a duty to permit entry that follows the Division (s 89(1)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- It says nothing about the renter having to be present, and nothing about a rebooking fee [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent in writing** which section of the Act the entry is under and where the $90 fee comes from. The retrieved documents contain no basis for it.
- **Check the notice.** On the older text, it should be in writing, say why entry is needed, and be posted or hand-delivered [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The same text lets a renter apply to the Tribunal for an order limiting when entry may occur (s 89(2)–(3)). It also lets a renter apply to the Tribunal if entry doesn't follow the rules (s 91) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Treat both as unconfirmed for today.
- **Confirm current rules with Consumer Affairs Victoria** (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting), which the Regulations point renters to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Check the current version of the Act's Division 8 on entry.

I haven't answered either part of your question definitively, because the in-force documents I retrieved don't cover it.

It applies the 8 a.m.–6 p.m. window only to delivering the notice, and it treats all the entry rules as unconfirmed for today.
