question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

I've used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 111 (file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", dated 25 November 2025). The metadata shows it was in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026, so it covers 15 January 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I haven't applied version 115 (13 October 2026), because it post-dates your question [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**1. A free payment method must be reasonably available (s 42(4)).** The rental provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs, other than your own bank or account fees, is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A fee-free bank transfer is likely to meet this. The Act doesn't say whether "reasonably available" takes account of speed, so I can't say whether "slower" matters.

**2. Fee disclosure (s 42(7)).** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, expressly including third party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees, before you consent to use that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**3. Charges barred for electronic payment facilities (s 51(3)(b)).** Section 51(3)(b) applies to "a person". It says no one may demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card fee charged through a rent app could fall under this wording. The Act doesn't define "electronic payment facility" in the text I retrieved, so I can't confirm it does.

**4. Rent payment fees by businesses (s 51A).** A person carrying on a business must not demand or receive a fee for any *prescribed matter* in relation to the payment of rent. The exceptions are the rental provider, the provider's agent, and authorised deposit-taking institutions (banks and similar) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who receives the fee?

Possibly, but the documents don't settle it.

- **Fee goes to the payments company.** The company is a business that isn't the provider, the agent or (presumably) a bank. So s 51A would apply to it, but only if the card fee is a "prescribed matter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The prescribed matters are set by regulations, and the regulations I retrieved are not the version in force on 15 January 2026. I can't confirm whether card fees are listed.
- **Fee goes to the agent.** The agent is carved out of s 51A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but s 51(3) still applies to "a person", and the agent's duties under s 42(4) and (7) still apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51(3)(b).** It doesn't distinguish by who receives the charge, so the destination of the fee doesn't change it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Answer:** the retrieved documents don't give a definite yes or no. Section 51(3)(b) could prohibit the card fee, and s 51A could prohibit it if the regulations prescribe it. The documents don't confirm either point.

## What you can do

- **Ask for the fee information in writing.** Ask the agent to set out all costs of each payment method, including the card fee, as s 42(7) requires before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Use the fee-free bank transfer** if you want to avoid the fee. The agent must keep a no-cost method reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent to confirm** whether the card fee is a charge for an "electronic payment facility" under s 51(3)(b), and whether it is a prescribed fee under s 51A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Raise it if the free option isn't reasonably available.** If the bank transfer is impractical for you, you can put that to the agent under s 42(4) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

I can't say from these documents where to take a complaint, or which regulations list the prescribed matters in force on 15 January 2026.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the first point, saying a fee-free bank transfer 'is likely to meet this' under s 42(4). It misses the second point. It never says the rent-payment fee ban (reg 21C) is not yet in effect on 15 January 2026 or that it applies from 31 March 2026. It only says it 'can't confirm whether card fees are listed' and even suggests the fee could be prohibited, which leaves the reader unable to tell which way it falls.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the card fee is already banned under s 51A or reg 21C, saying instead that s 51A 'could prohibit it if the regulations prescribe it' and 'The documents don't confirm either point', and it affirms that a fee-free option is required ('The rental provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs... is reasonably available to you').

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
# Damp, mould and rotting timber before moving in (as at 15 October 2019)

I applied the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088** (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019. Authorised Version No. 089 only starts on 4 December 2019, so I haven't used it.

## What the law says

- **Before you move in (s 65).** The landlord must ensure that on the agreed move-in day the premises are "vacant and in a reasonably clean condition". [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **If they aren't.** You are not required to enter into occupation. You also don't have to pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually move in. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Ongoing repairs (s 68).** The landlord must ensure the premises are "maintained in good repair". [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**Caveat:** s 65 is worded around "vacant" and "reasonably clean". It doesn't mention damp, mould or rotting timber. Whether mould counts as "not reasonably clean" isn't answered in the documents I found. The s 68 good-repair duty is the clearer fit for rotting timber and damp.

## Your options

**1. Not moving in yet.**
- If s 65 applies, you can decline to occupy. You owe no rent for the period before you actually move in. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**2. Asking for repairs.**
- **Written notice.** Give the landlord written notice of the non-urgent repairs needed. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **After 14 days.** If the repairs aren't done within 14 days of the notice, you can apply in writing to the Director (Consumer Affairs) to investigate. The Director must investigate, may negotiate arrangements for repairs, and must give you a written report. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Tribunal.** If you have the Director's report and are still not satisfied, you can apply to the Tribunal. You must apply within 60 days of receiving the report. If you haven't received the report within 90 days of applying for it, you can apply without it. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Tribunal orders.** If the Tribunal finds the landlord is in breach of the duty to maintain, it may order specified repairs. The order must state the repairs and the time to carry them out. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Rent Special Account.** After you've given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay your rent into the Rent Special Account. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Urgent repairs.** You can arrange these yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and couldn't. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less. You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. You can also apply to the Tribunal for an urgent-repairs order if you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $1000, or the landlord refuses to pay. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The definition of "urgent repairs" (s 3) wasn't in the text I retrieved, so I can't say whether mould or rotting timber qualifies.

**3. Asking for lower rent.**
- **Rent for the delay.** If s 65 applies, no rent is payable until you actually enter into occupation. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Excessive rent.** You can complain to the Director about excessive rent only where the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services or facilities, or after receiving a rent increase notice. The Tribunal can then declare rent excessive, taking into account "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises". [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Neither trigger obviously fits your situation, so a general rent reduction for poor condition is not clearly available on these documents.
- **Compensation.** The text I found for this version doesn't give a Tribunal power to order compensation for the repair breach. The compensation wording appears only as a later amendment in the endnotes. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**4. Cancelling the lease.**
- The sections of this version that I retrieved don't set out a tenant's right to cancel or end the agreement for this reason. They only say you needn't enter occupation under s 65 and needn't pay the pre-occupation rent. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- I can't say from these documents whether you can terminate. I'd suggest checking with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenant advocacy service before you act, as getting this wrong could expose you to liability.

## Practical steps
- Put the defects in writing to the landlord or agent and keep photos and dates.
- Say clearly that you haven't taken occupation because of them.
- Keep your written notice for the repair process above.

It also does not tie the right to cancel to disrepair or unfitness rather than mere uncleanliness, and it does not say that serious, unsafe damage can be urgent repairs.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the rental minimum standards or a mould and damp standard applied on 15 October 2019, and it does not say the renter must move in and pay rent; instead it relies on s 65 and s 68 of Authorised Version No. 088 and says 'You are not required to enter into occupation' and 'You owe no rent for the period before you actually move in.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088" (file rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, link 97-109aa088), which was in force on 15 October 2019. Every rule it applies comes from that version: s 65, s 68, the repair-notice, Director and Tribunal process, the $1000 urgent-repair cap, the excessive-rent triggers and the Rent Special Account. It does not apply any not-yet-commenced 2018 amendment. It says it cannot tell whether mould counts as an urgent repair, and it mentions the later compensation wording only to say it is not part of this version.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Documents used:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

- **Act:** the file metadata gives version 101, in force from 7 Sept 2022 to 23 May 2023, so it covers 8 Nov 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The excerpt I retrieved doesn't show the words "Authorised Version No." I'm taking "101" from the file name and metadata.
- **Regulations:** the file metadata gives version 002, in force from 1 June 2022 to 30 Nov 2024, so it also covers 8 Nov 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Where and how rent is paid:** rent is payable at the place in the agreement. If no place is specified, it is payable at the rented premises. It is paid in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing the payment method:** the rental provider and renter "by agreement" may change how rent is payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). My reading is that new bank details change the agreed manner of payment, so you can ask for the change in writing before you agree. The documents don't say this in so many words.
- **No-extra-cost option:** the provider or their agent must make sure a payment method with no extra costs is reasonably available to you. Your own bank fees are the only cost allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Cost information:** they must tell you about any costs of a payment method before you consent to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** whoever receives your rent must give you a written receipt if you pay in person. If you don't pay in person, they must give one within 5 business days of a request made when you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed and must state [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf):
  - your name and the premises;
  - the date of receipt;
  - the period paid for;
  - the amount;
  - that the payment is for rent.
- **Records:** if no receipt is required, the person must keep a record of the payment for up to 12 months. If you ask for a copy, they must provide it within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Change of details:** the prescribed Form 1 agreement says the rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the provider's or agent's details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This applies if your agreement is on that form.

## What you can check or ask

1. **Look at your agreement.** Check the "Payment details" and preferred payment methods in the standard terms (clause 8 of Form 1) and the rental provider and agent details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Compare them with the new bank details.
2. **Ask for the change in writing.** Ask for written notice of the new management arrangement and the new account. The 7-day notice rule in Form 1 supports this [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Confirm who the new payee is.** Confirm that the account name matches the owner named in your agreement. The documents don't explain how to verify an account or detect fraud. I can't say more on that from them.
4. **Ask about costs.** Ask whether the new method has any fees and whether a no-extra-cost option is available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Request a receipt.** Ask for a receipt for each payment. Make the request when you pay, so the 5-business-day deadline applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check your bond.** The bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of payment. The RTBA sends a receipt. If you have no receipt within 15 business days of paying, you can email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A change in who manages the property is a good reason to check that this receipt arrived.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't require you to be home for a smoke alarm check. They also don't mention a $90 rebooking fee, so I can't confirm whether it is allowed. The applicable versions are the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Version 111 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 Version 005 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), both in force on 3 December 2025.

### What the law says about entry

- **Who can enter and when:** A provider or their agent may enter, with any necessary persons, at any time agreed with the renter if the renter consented within 7 days before entry. Otherwise, entry is allowed between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice:** For a duty under the Act, such as a smoke alarm check, at least 24 hours' notice is required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Seven days' notice is more than enough. The notice must be in writing, state why entry is wanted, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. weekday window falls within the permitted hours.
- **Your duty:** A renter must permit entry that complies with the Act, but a renter can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order specifying or limiting when entry may occur [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Conduct:** The person entering must act reasonably and must not stay longer than necessary without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Smoke alarms:** The provider must ensure smoke alarms are working, have batteries, and are tested at least once every 12 months. Mains-powered smoke alarms must be tested, repaired or replaced by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to be there?

The retrieved excerpts don't say whether a renter must be present during an entry. They only say you must permit entry that follows the Act's procedure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Having a key does not in itself grant entry rights. The entry must still meet the notice, timing and manner requirements above. The documents don't address whether you can ask for a different time, other than through a VCAT application.

### Can they charge $90?

The retrieved documents contain no provision for a rebooking fee for a missed entry. I can't say whether it is lawful, and I'm not able to answer that from these sources. The Act does prohibit a provider from demanding fees for consent to assignment or sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but that does not cover this situation.

### What you can do

1. **Check the notice:** Confirm it is in writing, states the reason for entry, and was delivered properly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Consider the time window:** If you can't attend, ask the agent to agree to a different time. Entry is allowed at any agreed time if you consented within 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for the fee's basis:** Ask the agent in writing which provision of the Act or your agreement authorises the $90 charge.
4. **Seek VCAT:** If you want to limit when entry occurs, you can apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A renter may also apply for an order restraining entry if the provider fails to comply with the entry rules [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

For the hardest point, the answer says "The retrieved documents don't require you to be home for a smoke alarm check" and that the provider or agent "may enter, with any necessary persons" on notice, so the renter's duty is only to permit entry. It also states that smoke alarm testing is the provider's duty, needing at least 24 hours' written notice between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., which "Seven days' notice is more than enough" to satisfy.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must be home or must pay the fee; it says "The retrieved documents don't require you to be home for a smoke alarm check" and "I can't say whether it is lawful" about the $90 charge.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 15 January 2026, the documents suggest the app company probably cannot charge you a card fee for paying rent, but the position is not fully settled. The documents also don't say who the fee goes to is irrelevant, and they don't define key terms.

## What the law says

- **The agent must offer a no-extra-cost option.** The rental provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to you. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **You must be told about fees first.** The provider or agent must give you information about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, before you consent to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Charges for electronic payment facilities are restricted.** A person must not demand or receive a charge from a renter in relation to the use of any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent (penalty: 60 penalty units) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This wording is broad enough to cover a card fee, but the documents don't say whether a card is an "electronic payment facility" in this sense.
- **Fees for rent payment are restricted, with a carve-out.** A business that is not a provider, provider's agent or authorised deposit-taking institution must not demand or receive a fee for a prescribed matter relating to paying rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The payments company is not one of the excluded persons [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the prescribed matters are listed in regulation 21C, which only takes effect on 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That regulation excludes "payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents do not identify any Act that permits such surcharges.
- **Agreement terms.** A term requiring rent to be paid in advance by a method with additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Version and date:** On 15 January 2026, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) apply. Regulation 21C is not yet in effect on this date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

The documents suggest it matters for which rule applies, but the obligations point in the same direction:

- **If the agent receives any part of the fee,** the agent is directly bound by the no-extra-cost duty and the charge restriction [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **If only the app company keeps the fee,** the restriction on charging for rent payment still applies to it as a business that is not an excluded person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Its liability for a rent payment fee depends on regulation 21C, which is not in force yet [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The agent still has the duty to ensure a no-extra-cost method is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), even if a third party charges the fee.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** what costs the card option carries, as the agent must disclose these before you choose it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for the bank transfer option to be made available** and confirm that the agent is required to ensure a no-extra-cost method is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents do not define "reasonably available," so a slower method may or may not meet this test.
3. **Ask for a receipt** for each rent payment. You can request one, and it must be given within 5 business days of the request if you don't pay in person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check your agreement.** If it requires a payment method with extra costs, it may be a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't set out how to enforce these rights or complain about a breach beyond the penalties mentioned above. If you need that, you'll need to check other sources.

must-mention.reason: Yes: both points are covered. The answer says the agent must ensure a no-extra-cost method is "reasonably available" and that the slower transfer "may or may not meet this test," which matches the rubric's own "may satisfy" hedge. It also states that "Regulation 21C is not yet in effect on this date" and that it "only takes effect on 31 March 2026." Its overall leaning that the fee is "probably" not allowed is muddled, but that does not remove either required point.

The answer does not claim the card fee is already banned on 15 January 2026 under s 51A or reg 21C: it hedges ('probably cannot charge you a card fee... but the position is not fully settled') and says 'Its liability for a rent payment fee depends on regulation 21C, which is not in force yet.' It also affirms a fee-free rule exists ('The rental provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs... is reasonably available to you').

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025' and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025'. Its links (97-109aa111, 21-3sra005) confirm both versions. It relies on no other version and correctly treats reg 21C as not yet in effect.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088 (in force 2 July to 3 December 2019, so it applies on 15 October 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), you may be able to end the agreement before moving in, and the landlord must fix the defects. The documents do not clearly support a rent reduction. They say you need not pay rent for the period before you can move in, but that is not the same as a general rent cut.

**What the law says**

- **Landlord's duty on the handover day:** The landlord must ensure that on the day you are to enter occupation, the premises are vacant and reasonably clean. You are not required to move in if they do not comply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent before moving in:** If the premises do not comply, you are not required to pay rent from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain:** The landlord must ensure the premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp:** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure", including "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This version also contains amending text that changes this definition, but the documents do not clearly show whether that amendment was in operation on 15 October 2019.
- **Condition report:** Before you enter occupation, the landlord must give you two copies of a condition report stating the state of repair and general condition of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you are not given one, you may complete one and give it to the landlord between inspecting the premises and 5 business days after entering occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**Your options**

1. **Cancel:** Under section 226, a tenancy terminates if the tenant has not entered into possession and has given the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair" or "unfit for human habitation" (among other grounds) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Whether collecting the keys counts as "entering into possession" is not addressed in the documents, so this needs checking before you rely on it.
   - Alternatively, section 238 allows a tenant to give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are "unfit for human habitation" or destroyed or unsafe. The notice may specify a termination date that is the date it is given or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Section 238 is not limited to premises you have not yet entered, but its application to your situation is not confirmed.

2. **Ask for repairs:**
   - Notify the landlord in writing. A renter must give written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - **Urgent repairs:** If the landlord cannot or does not carry out urgent repairs after you have taken reasonable steps to arrange them, you may arrange them. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether this applies before you have moved in.
   - **Non-urgent repairs:** You may apply to the Director to investigate if you have given written notice and the landlord has not carried out the repairs within 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You may apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring specified repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

3. **Ask for lower rent:** The documents do not provide a direct route to reduce rent for defects. The Tribunal can make a rent order that considers the state of repair and general condition of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), which may be relevant if you pursue a rent dispute. The only specific rent protection in the documents is the rent-free period before you move in, described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Rent paid into the Rent Special Account is linked to repair notices, but the documents do not clearly show how this applies before occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether you have "entered into possession" by collecting keys (this affects section 226).
- How the lease terms affect your rights.
- Whether the urgent repair and rent account provisions apply before you move in.
- Whether the amendments changing the urgent repairs definition were in operation on 15 October 2019.

Because cancelling a lease can have significant consequences, consider getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer before serving any notice. This suggestion is general and not from the documents.

The condition report is mentioned only as a general procedure, not as proof for the termination ground. The other two points are covered: the s 226 notice ground before taking possession, and the landlord's duty to maintain in good repair, with mould and damp as possible urgent repairs.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Don't pay into the new account until the change is agreed in writing and you've checked it. The Act lets the owner and renter change the payment method by agreement, not by one side's notice. As of 8 November 2022, the governing text is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 101, in force from 7 September 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), read with the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 002, in force from 1 June 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Where and how rent is paid:** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the rented premises if none is specified. Otherwise it is payable in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing the payment method:** The landlord and renter, *by agreement*, may change the manner in which rent is payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Act does not allow the owner to change it unilaterally.
- **Costs:** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using it, including third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Fee-free option:** The provider or agent must ensure a payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than your bank or account fees) is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Centrepay must also be permitted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** For rent paid other than in person, you can request a written receipt, which must be given within 5 business days. It must be signed and state your name and the rented premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Contact changes:** The provider must notify you in writing of any change to the agent's or provider's contact details within 7 days of the change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond:** The bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days after it is received, and the provider must give you a bond lodgment form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If the provider assigns or transfers their rights and duties to another person and a bond has been paid, both must notify the Authority within 5 days, and the provider must give you a copy of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Check your lease.** Look for the clause on where and how rent is paid. If it names the agent's account, the owner cannot simply substitute theirs without an agreed change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for the change in writing.** Ask the agent to confirm, in writing, that the owner is now the rental provider and that you agree to the new payment method. Don't rely on a phone call or an unverified message with new bank details.
3. **Confirm the account details.** Check that the account name matches the owner named in the agreement or in the written notice, and verify the details through a channel you already trust (for example, by calling a number you already have, not one in the message).
4. **Ask about costs.** Find out whether the new method carries fees. You're entitled to that information before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask for a receipt.** Every rent payment should produce a receipt that meets the content requirements above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check the bond.** Confirm the bond is held by the Authority. If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, you may notify the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Since the bond was paid about a week ago, you may not be past that point yet. Ask whether the owner's takeover involves any transfer of the agreement, because a transfer triggers the 5-day notification to the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
7. **Check the form.** The payment clause in the regulations' standard form requires at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees), and Centrepay or another electronic transfer option [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That form is for agreements of more than 5 years, so it may not match your lease. Check which form your agreement uses.

## What the documents don't cover

The documents don't say how to verify a bank account or whether a change of manager needs a new agreement. They also don't cover what to do if the change turns out to be a scam. question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, you have a duty to let the agent in, but the retrieved extracts don't say you must be home yourself. The Act doesn't appear to allow a $90 rebooking fee for a missed entry. This is based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 111, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025), which was in force on 3 December 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Right of entry:** The provider or agent may enter, together with necessary persons, for a purpose such as carrying out a duty under the Act. For those purposes, entry is allowed between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Testing smoke alarms is one such duty. Smoke alarms must be "tested at least once every 12 months" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A 7-day notice exceeds the minimum, and 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. falls inside the permitted hours.
- **Notice requirements:** The notice must be in writing, state why entry is wanted, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Check how the notice was delivered.
- **Your duty:** You "has a duty to permit a person exercising a right of entry in accordance with this Division to enter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations summarise this as: "The renter must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Being present:** The extracts I retrieved don't require you to be home. They do say the person entering "must do so in a reasonable manner" and must not stay longer than necessary without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The $90 fee:** The extracts contain no provision allowing a rebooking fee for a missed entry. A person "must not demand or accept from a renter who has failed to comply with" the agreement or the Act any payment other than rent or an amount the Act provides for. The penalty for a natural person is 150 penalty units [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Regulations also say additional terms "must not exclude, restrict or modify any of the rights and duties included in the Act" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

1. **Ask the agent for the legal basis** of the $90 charge in writing. Don't pay until you have an answer.
2. **Ask for a different time** or agree one. You can also apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order specifying or limiting when entry may occur [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Be home if you can**, to avoid a dispute. If you can't, you can still permit entry at the agreed time. The documents don't address the agent's use of the key when you are absent, so ask the agent to confirm how they will enter.
4. **Seek further help** from Consumer Affairs Victoria at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** The extracts don't address whether a renter must be present during an inspection, how the agent may use a key when the renter is absent, or whether a rebooking fee is ever lawful. I also couldn't confirm the notice was properly delivered, or whether any tenancy-specific terms in your agreement mention fees. Please check your agreement and get specific advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT.

**Sources**
- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 111 (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025).
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021, version 005 (rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025).
- [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 111 (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025), section 505.

Point 2: it says "Testing smoke alarms is one such duty," with "at least 24 hours' notice" in writing between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., and "A 7-day notice exceeds the minimum."

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the card fee is probably not allowed in the way you describe, but the answer depends partly on who collects it. The documents don't fully settle the second part.

Both sources below were in force on 15 January 2026: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 005, in force from 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **The agent must offer a no-extra-cost option.** A provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter." The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed.** The provider or agent must give information about costs, including "third party transaction fees", before the renter consents to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fees by businesses are restricted.** A person carrying on a business, other than specified persons such as a provider or agent, must not demand or receive a fee for a prescribed matter relating to rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **The prescribed rent-payment fee rule starts later.** The regulation that lists "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter says it "has effect on and after 31 March 2026" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So on 15 January 2026 that regulation is not yet in force, and I can't confirm from these documents what rent-payment fees were prescribed before then.

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

- **Yes, it matters for the fee-collection rule.** The restriction in s 51A applies to businesses other than specified persons, and the agent is a specified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved are cut off before the full list of specified persons, so I can't confirm whether your payments company is covered.
- **It matters less for the agent's duty.** Whoever collects the fee, the agent must still ensure a no-extra-cost method is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A bank transfer with no fee is the kind of method that duty refers to, but the documents don't say whether a slower method is "reasonably available". They don't address processing speed at all.
- **The agreement's terms also matter.** The agreement sets the payment manner, and a term requiring rent to be paid in advance by a method with additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

1. Ask the agent in writing what the card fee is, who receives it, and what other payment methods are available. The agent must give you this cost information before you consent to the card method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. Check your tenancy agreement for the payment methods it lists and whether it requires card payment.
3. Ask the agent whether the bank transfer option is reasonably available to you and whether it is included in the agreement.

I can't tell from these documents whether the fee is lawful right now, what the complaint process is, or whether your payments company is a specified person. You may want to check those points with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advisory service.

The answer says the agent 'must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs... is reasonably available' and calls a fee-free bank transfer 'the kind of method that duty refers to'. question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Which law applies:** The retrieved document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088 (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf"), which is in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That covers 15 October 2019. The file also contains amending text from the *Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2018* (No. 45/2018) that changes wording and adds new sections [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't say when those changes commenced, so I rely on the Act's own wording below. Where I mention amended text, I say so.

## What the law says

- **Premises must be ready on move-in day.** The landlord must ensure that, on the day the tenant is to enter occupation, the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition. A tenant is not required to move into premises that don't comply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **No rent until you can move in.** If the premises don't comply, the tenant doesn't have to pay rent from the agreed occupation day until the day they actually enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain good repair.** The landlord must ensure the premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Whether your problems qualify:** The documents don't define damp, mould or rotting timber as a breach by themselves. The "urgent repairs" definition covers any fault or damage that makes rented premises "unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Amended text also lists "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" as a case of unsafe or insecure premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but I can't confirm that this applied on 15 October 2019. Whether your specific defects meet these tests is a factual question the documents don't answer.

## Your options

**1. Cancel (terminate the lease)**
- The tenancy terminates if the tenant has not entered possession and gives the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or are unavailable for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Your situation fits the "not entered into possession" condition, but the excerpts don't say whether collecting the keys counts as taking possession.
- The excerpts don't specify the form, content or timing of the termination notice.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to carry them out immediately and the landlord can't be reached or doesn't act. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, or $1000, whichever is less, after 14 days' written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can also apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order requiring urgent repairs. The Tribunal must hear it within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give the landlord written notice that repairs are required. If they aren't carried out within 14 days, you may apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can then apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the Director's report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order the landlord to carry out specified repairs and specify the time for completion [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The excerpts don't say whether these repair routes work before you have moved in.

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The most direct answer is the rent-free period described above: you pay no rent until you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal can set a rent amount that is considered reasonable. Its considerations include the state of repair and general condition of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If it makes such an order, the landlord cannot require rent above that amount for 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can also order a refund of the difference [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The excerpt cuts off the opening wording of this provision, so I can't confirm the full test or who may apply.

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether picking up the keys counts as "entering into possession."
- The required form and timing of a termination notice.
- Whether damp, mould and rotting timber are a breach of the duty to maintain good repair in your case.
- Whether the repair and rent processes apply before you move in.
- Bond, compensation and any amounts you have already paid.

Because some of these points are unclear and the amended wording may matter, consider getting advice from a tenancy service or the Tribunal before you give any notice.

All three points are covered: the answer says the tenancy ends if a tenant who 'has not entered possession' gives notice 'on the ground that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or are unavailable for occupation'. It states the landlord's duty to maintain good repair, sets out repair requests, and notes that urgent repairs cover damage making premises 'unsafe or insecure'. By tying cancellation to the disrepair or unfitness grounds, separate from the 'reasonably clean' move-in requirement, it shows that cancellation turns on disrepair or unfitness rather than mere uncleanliness.

It uses this to frame whether the user's damp and mould qualify for the urgent-repair route, with only a caveat that it 'can't confirm that this applied on 15 October 2019', so the answer relies on a rule that was not in force on that date.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 8 November 2022, the owner can't unilaterally change how you pay rent. Check the points below before you pay anything into the new account.

## What the law says

- **Rent payment is set by your agreement.** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the rented premises if none is specified. Otherwise, it is payable in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing the payment method requires agreement.** The provider and renter, "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed first.** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs (including third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees) you may incur with a payment method before you consent to using it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **A no-extra-cost method must be available.** A method that incurs no additional costs (other than your own bank or account fees) must be reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider must also permit Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **You are entitled to a receipt.** If you pay by a method other than in person and request a receipt, it must be given within 5 business days. It must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond rules.** The provider or agent must give the bond to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (the Authority) within 10 business days after receiving it, with the completed bond lodgment form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Authority must send a receipt within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, you may notify the Authority [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Until the bond is paid to the Authority, the provider holds it on trust for you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Transfers must be notified.** If a provider assigns or transfers their rights and duties under the agreement, the provider and the new person must notify the Authority within 5 days, and the provider must give you a copy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether an owner taking over from an agent counts as a transfer in this sense.
- **Contact changes must be notified.** The provider must give you written notice of any change to their agent or contact information before the end of 7 days after the change .

## What to check or ask before paying

1. **Get the change in writing and agreed by you.** Ask for a written variation. Under the law, a change to the payment method needs your agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Don't treat an agent's message as a unilateral change.
2. **Check the fees.** Ask what costs, if any, apply to the new payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Confirm the method is fee-free apart from your own bank fees, since that's the standard the law sets [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the payment method is permitted.** Ask whether the new arrangement allows Centrepay or another electronic method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Confirm who the payee is.** Ask who owns the account and why the owner is now collecting rent. The agent's notice should identify the owner and agent contact details, and any change to those details must be notified in writing within 7 days .
5. **Confirm your bond status.** Ask for the bond lodgment form and confirm it was lodged with the Authority within 10 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Check whether you have received the Authority's receipt, which should come within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If it hasn't come within 15 business days of your payment, you can contact the Authority [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The regulations list the Authority's email as rtba@justice.vic.gov.au and its phone number as 1300 137 164 .
6. **Get a receipt for each rent payment.** Request one if you don't pay in person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
7. **Confirm the bank details independently.** The documents don't cover how to verify bank account changes or protect against payment fraud. As a general precaution (not from the sources), confirm the new details by calling a number you already have for the agency or owner, not one provided in the new message.

## Limits of the documents

The documents don't say whether changing bank account details, with no change in payment method, counts as a change "by agreement" under the rent payment rules. They also don't say whether an agent-to-owner handover is a transfer that triggers the 5-day Authority notice. Ask the agent or owner to clarify these points, or seek advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or the Authority.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether you must be home. They do say you must allow lawful entry, and they don't appear to authorise a $90 rebooking fee. - **Right of entry:** An agent may enter, with any necessary persons, at any time between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, if at least 24 hours' notice is given for a purpose under s 86(1)(c) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entry to carry out a duty under the Act falls under s 86(1)(c) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The provider's smoke alarm duty is that alarms are tested at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice:** The notice must be in writing and state why entry is wanted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your 7-day written notice for a smoke alarm check fits the time limits. Your 10 a.m.–12:30 p.m. window also falls within 8 a.m.–6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The retrieved provisions don't expressly require a weekday, so the weekday limit is a term of the agent's notice, not a statutory requirement I can find.
- **Your duty:** A renter has a duty to permit entry in accordance with the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Being present:** The retrieved documents don't say whether you must personally attend. They also don't say whether the agent may enter without you. Having a key doesn't in itself override the Act's notice and timing rules [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee:** The retrieved documents contain no provision allowing a fee to rebook an entry. I can't confirm from these documents whether the $90 charge is lawful or not.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check the notice:** Confirm it is in writing and states the reason for entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for different times:** Entry must be in a reasonable manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT for an order specifying or limiting the days, times and purposes of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations also say the renter must allow entry only where the provider has followed proper procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
3. **If the agent breaches the rules:** You can apply to VCAT for an order restraining future entry if the provider doesn't comply with the entry rules [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Damage to your goods during entry can also support a compensation application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get guidance:** The Regulations point to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for more information [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
