question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 15 January 2026, the agent must make a fee-free payment method reasonably available and must disclose card fees before you choose a method. The documents I found don't show a ban on this specific card fee yet, because the rule that would prohibit it doesn't start until 31 March 2026.

## What the law says

- **Fee-free method must be available.** The agent (or the rental provider) "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Fees must be disclosed.** The agent must tell you about costs, "including third party transaction fees," that you may incur by using a particular payment method, "before the renter consents to use the payment method." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Bank transfer is the prescribed method.** For the purposes of the rent payment rules, "the prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) A manual bank transfer is therefore the method the regulations point to.
- **Fees charged by a business.** A business other than a rental provider, an agent, or a bank must not "demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to ... the payment of rent." The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The app company is not one of the exempt persons, so this provision is the one that would apply to it.
- **The gap.** The prescribed matters are listed in regulation 21C, which includes "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)." But regulation 21C "has effect on and after 31 March 2026." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) As of 15 January 2026, the retrieved documents don't show that this list applies yet. The documents also don't identify any other Act that permits a payment surcharge.

## Your questions

**Can the app charge the card fee?** On the retrieved documents, I can't give a definitive yes or no. The fee-free-method and disclosure duties apply now [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but the specific ban on rent-payment fees under section 51A only gets its content from regulation 21C, which starts on 31 March 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Once that starts, the documents indicate that a card fee charged by a non-exempt business would likely fall within the ban, unless another Act permits it.

**Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?** Yes, but mainly for the fee ban:
- If the **app company** keeps the fee, it is not an exempt person under section 51A, so the ban (once in force) would apply to it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- If the **agent** receives the fee, it is an exempt person under section 51A, so that ban does not apply to it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) However, the agent still has to make a fee-free method reasonably available and disclose fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Those duties apply whoever receives the money.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing** to confirm that a fee-free method (bank transfer/EFT) is available, and to state what fees the card option involves. The agent must give that information before you agree to use a payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. **Choose bank transfer.** It is the prescribed method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), and the regulations don't require it to be fast. Any delay is a matter for your agreement, which the documents don't cover.
3. **Ask who receives the card fee.** This affects whether the section 51A ban can apply once it starts on 31 March 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
4. **Check the latest version of the regulations.** The retrieved version of the regulations runs only until 9 February 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so it may have been replaced before the 31 March 2026 start date. The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 version I retrieved runs until 29 June 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The documents I have don't cover complaint or enforcement steps (for example, to the Director or VCAT), so I can't advise on those from them.

**Document versions used:**
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, version 111, in force from 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, S.R. No. 3/2021, version 005, in force from 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088 (incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), you have grounds to refuse to move in, to require repairs, and to withhold rent for the period before you move in. Cancelling is probably available, but the documents I retrieved don't confirm which version of the cancellation provision applies on 15 October 2019.

**What the law says**

- **Condition on the day you take occupation:** The landlord must ensure that on the agreed day you enter occupation, the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition. If they don't comply, you are "not required to enter into occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **No rent before you move in:** If the premises don't comply, you are not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed day until the day you actually enter occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repair duty:** The landlord must ensure the premises are "maintained in good repair." The 2018 amendment text in the same document says the landlord must provide and maintain premises "in good repair; and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation," and that this applies "whether or not the renter was aware of any disrepair... before entering into occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp:** The definition of "urgent repairs" includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Rotting timber may also fall under the "unsafe or insecure" limb, but the documents don't say so expressly.

**Your options**

1. **Cancel:**
   - The amendment text in the document says a renter who has not entered possession may terminate by giving notice on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair" or "unfit for human habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The same text allows a renter to give a notice of intention to vacate where premises are "unfit for human habitation," with a termination date that may be the date of the notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - However, that text appears in the endnotes amendment section, and the consolidated provisions listed in the table of contents (for example, s 226, "Termination by tenant before possession") were not in the excerpts I retrieved. I can't confirm from these documents whether the new wording was in force on 15 October 2019. Check this before relying on it.

2. **Ask for repairs:**
   - Give the landlord **written notice** of the damage as soon as practicable. The Act requires this of a renter who becomes aware of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to carry them out immediately and you cannot get them done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The reimbursement terms have changed between the old and amended text. The old text caps reimbursement at the lesser of the reasonable cost or $1000, while the amendment text requires reimbursement of the reasonable cost within 7 days of written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Because you have not moved in, this route may be less practical, and I would not carry out work yourself without advice.
   - **Non-urgent repairs:** Give written notice, and if the landlord does not carry out the repairs within 14 days, you may apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You may then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order specified repairs and the time for them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

3. **Lower the rent:**
   - You may pay no rent for the period before you actually move in, as described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - The Tribunal can also assess whether rent is excessive. In doing so it considers "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). An order can stop the landlord requiring rent above the amount ordered for 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - The excerpts I retrieved do not include the full procedure for complaining to the Director or applying to the Tribunal about excessive rent (sections 45 and 46), so I can't set out those steps from the documents.

**Not covered by the documents:** Your specific lease terms, your bond, whether any lease break fee applies, and what happens to any rent you have already paid. The documents also don't say how the Tribunal would treat your situation given that you have not yet moved in. Before acting, get tenancy advice and keep photos, written communications and a dated record of the defects.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer says a renter who has not entered possession may terminate by notice on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair" or "unfit for human habitation", and names s 226. Its caveat about the in-force version still concludes "Cancelling is probably available," so a reader can tell which way it falls. (2) It states the landlord's duty to keep the premises "maintained in good repair", explains how to request repairs, and notes that mould or damp making the premises unsafe falls within urgent repairs. (3) It ties cancellation to disrepair or unfitness, separate from the cleanliness rule, and advises keeping "photos, written communications and a dated record of the defects."

It quotes the 'urgent repairs' definition, which mentions mould, but that is not an assertion that a minimum standard applies, and it flags uncertainty about which amended provisions were in force on that date ('I can't confirm from these documents whether the new wording was in force on 15 October 2019'). It also does not say the renter must move in and pay rent; it says the opposite: 'you are "not required to enter into occupation"' and 'you are not required to pay rent for the period from the agreed day until the day you actually enter occupation'.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer correctly names "Authorised Version No. 088 (incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019)", but it applies rules from the not-yet-in-force 2018 amendments as the law, including mould or damp as an urgent repair, the "reasonably fit and suitable" repair duty, and the not-in-good-repair or unfit-for-habitation termination ground offered as a step the user can take. The caveat on the termination ground does not cure this, and deleting that material would change the answer's substance.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 8 November 2022, the owner can't change how you pay rent just by sending new bank details. The change needs your agreement, and you should check the points below before paying.

## What the law says

- **Changing the payment method needs agreement.** The renter and the rental provider "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [1, *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 101, in force 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023]. The agent can't make this change alone, and the agent is also a "residential rental provider" under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Payment must be fee-free and reasonably available.** The provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed before you consent.** The provider must tell you about "any costs (including third party transaction fees, direct debit dishonour fees and any other electronic payment facility fees)" before you agree to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Centrepay and electronic funds transfer.** Providers must permit Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer [2, *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 002, in force 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024].
- **Receipts.** Rent payments must be receipted in writing. If you pay electronically, the receipt is due within 5 business days of payment, if you request one at the time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed and state your name, the premises, the date, the period covered, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond.** The provider must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Authority must send a receipt within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider holds the bond on trust for you until it is paid to the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Form 1 says that if you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Transfer of the landlord's rights.** If the provider assigns or transfers their rights and duties, the provider and the new person must notify the Authority within 5 days, and the provider must give you a copy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether moving from an agent to an owner-managed arrangement counts as a transfer.

## What to check before paying

1. **Get the change in writing and agreed.** Ask the owner to confirm the new account in writing and agree to it as a variation of your lease. The Act requires agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Confirm who the owner is.** The rental provider's name, address and contact details are required in the agreement. The provider must notify you within 7 days if the agent's details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask about fees.** Ask whether the new method has any costs. The owner must tell you about them before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
## What the law says

On **3 December 2025**, the applicable law was:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111**, incorporating amendments as at **25 November 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005**, in force from **25 November 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The rental provider must ensure smoke alarms are correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries and tested at least every 12 months. Mains-powered alarms must be tested by a suitably qualified person. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

An agent may enter to carry out a duty under the Act, including the smoke-alarm duty, if the renter has received **at least 7 days’ notice**. Entry must be between **8 am and 6 pm on a day other than a public holiday**. The notice must be in writing and state why entry is required. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

You have a duty to permit a person exercising that lawful right of entry to enter. The Act does **not** say that the renter must personally be at home. Therefore, if the agent has a key, the documents support the agent arranging lawful entry without you being present, provided the entry otherwise complies with the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** state that an agent may charge a **$90 rebooking fee** when a renter is not home. They also do not provide a specific rule authorising or prohibiting that fee. **On these documents alone, whether the $90 can be charged cannot be determined.** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Tell the agent in writing that:

1. you consent to the inspector entering during the notified period using the agent’s key; and  
2. you do not agree that your personal attendance is required.

Ask the agent to identify the legal or contractual basis for the **$90 fee**. Keep the notice and your correspondence. If the agent enters outside the permitted requirements, or otherwise fails to comply with the entry rules, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order limiting or restraining further entry. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No: the second point is missing because the answer misstates the notice rule. It says entry to carry out a duty requires "at least 7 days' notice", not the required at least 24 hours' written notice, which materially changes the law even though it correctly covers the landlord's smoke-alarm duty, the 8 am–6 pm window and that the renter need not be present.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing. It states that "The Act does **not** say that the renter must personally be at home," and on the fee it says "whether the $90 can be charged cannot be determined." It therefore neither requires the renter to be home nor says the $90 must be paid.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111" (link 97-109aa111) and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005" (link 21-3sra005), and every rule it applies is sourced only from those versions.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 January 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111**, in force from **25 November 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

- A rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional costs**—apart from the renter’s own bank or account fees—is **reasonably available**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Before the renter agrees to use a payment method, the rental provider or agent must provide information about costs, including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Separately, **a person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge or indemnity for a charge** relating to the establishment or use of an electronic payment facility for paying rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

On that wording, a card fee charged for using the rent app to pay rent appears to be prohibited, even if the fee is described as a third-party or payment-provider fee. The Act does not say that the result changes because the fee is paid to the app company rather than the agent: the prohibition applies to **“a person”** demanding or receiving the charge. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved documents do not explain how the reference to “third-party transaction fees” in the information requirement interacts with the separate prohibition on charges for using an electronic payment facility. They also do not define when a slower fee-free bank-transfer option is “reasonably available.” [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask or do

You can ask the agent and the app company to:

1. remove or refund the card fee, citing the prohibition on charges for using an electronic payment facility to pay rent; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. confirm in writing who demands or receives the fee and what it is said to cover; and [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
3. confirm that the fee-free bank-transfer method is reasonably available and provide the required information about all payment-method costs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The regulations’ prescribed rental-agreement form also states that the rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method and must allow electronic funds transfer or Centrepay. The applicable regulations document is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005**, in force on 15 January 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer misses the second point. It never says the specific rent-payment fee ban (reg 21C) does not yet apply on 15 January 2026, and does not mention the 31 March 2026 start date. Instead it concludes the opposite: 'a card fee charged for using the rent app to pay rent appears to be prohibited.' It also hedges on whether the slower fee-free bank transfer satisfies the 'reasonably available' requirement.

must-not-say.reason: No — the answer says that on 15 January 2026 "a card fee charged for using the rent app to pay rent appears to be prohibited, even if the fee is described as a third-party or payment-provider fee." It bases this on the rule that "a person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge... relating to the establishment or use of an electronic payment facility," which asserts that the card-fee ban (the s 51A / reg 21C prohibition) already applies on that date.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111' (link 97-109aa111) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005' (link 21-3sra005), and relies on no other version.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## Law applying on 15 October 2019

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Because you have not moved your belongings in or stayed there, the Act’s “before possession” rule appears relevant. Under section 226, a tenancy agreement terminates if the tenant has not entered into possession and gives the landlord a **notice of termination** stating that the premises are:

- not in good repair;
- unfit for human habitation;
- unsafe;
- not vacant;
- not legally available for residential use; or
- otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord must ensure that, on the agreed occupation day, the premises are vacant and reasonably clean. You are not required to enter premises that do not meet that requirement, and you do not have to pay rent for the period before you actually enter into occupation if the premises do not comply. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The landlord must also maintain the premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Cancel/terminate the tenancy:**  
   You can give the landlord a notice of termination under section 226, relying on the premises being **not in good repair** or, if the condition is sufficiently serious, **unfit for human habitation** or otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not state a required notice form or specify whether keys alone amount to entering into possession, so retain evidence that you had not moved in or occupied the house.

2. **Ask for repairs:**  
   You can notify the landlord in writing and ask for the damp, mould and rotting timber to be repaired. The landlord’s duty is to keep the premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord does not act within **14 days** after written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate; after receiving the Director’s report, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

   If the rotting timber or another defect makes the premises **unsafe**, it may fall within “urgent repairs”; the Act includes “any fault or damage that makes rented premises unsafe or insecure.” [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not specifically classify damp or mould as urgent repairs.

3. **Ask for lower rent:**  
   The retrieved provisions do **not** give a general right to reduce the agreed rent merely because defects are discovered before occupation. The excessive-rent process applies where the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services, facilities or other items, or where the tenant receives a notice of a rent increase; it is not stated to cover an initial rent reduction for these defects. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) You can ask the landlord to agree to a lower rent, but the documents do not establish that you can require it.

Do not simply stop paying rent after entering into occupation: the specific pre-occupation rent protection applies only for the period before you actually enter into occupation when the premises do not comply with section 65. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) Section 226 lets a tenant who has not entered possession terminate by notice where the premises are 'not in good repair' or 'unfit for human habitation'. (2) The landlord 'must also maintain the premises in good repair', the tenant can 'ask for the damp, mould and rotting timber to be repaired', and 'any fault or damage that makes rented premises unsafe' may be urgent repairs. (3) This is the hardest point and is covered only implicitly: the answer ties cancellation to the premises' condition, 'relying on the premises being not in good repair or, if the condition is sufficiently serious, unfit for human habitation'. It treats the 'reasonably clean' requirement separately, as a rent and entry issue rather than a ground for termination. It does not explicitly contrast this with mere uncleanliness or mention photos or an inspection as evidence.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the home must meet rental minimum standards or a mould and damp standard; it relies only on the 1997 Act duties, for example "The landlord must also maintain the premises in good repair." It also does not say the renter must move in and pay rent, and instead states "You can give the landlord a notice of termination under section 226."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019' and its link (97-109aa088), and every rule it applies comes from that pre-2021 version: s 226 termination before possession, vacant and reasonably clean on the occupation day, the good repair duty, the 14-day non-urgent repairs and Director/Tribunal process, the old urgent repairs definition, and excessive rent. It also expressly avoids the not-yet-operative amendment by saying the documents do not classify damp or mould as urgent repairs.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **8 November 2022**, the applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101 (in force from 7 September 2022)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002 (in force from 1 June 2022)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

- Rent must generally be paid in the manner specified in the residential rental agreement. The rental provider and renter may change that manner **by agreement**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- If the agency stops acting for the owner, the rental provider must give you written notice of the change in the relevant information **within 7 days**. If there is no agent, that notice must include the owner’s **full name and address for service of documents**, plus an **emergency telephone number for urgent repairs**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- The agreement’s payment section should identify the available rent-payment methods and payment details. It must provide at least one payment method with no additional cost other than your own bank or account fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you should do or ask before paying

1. **Check the signed lease**: confirm the stated rental provider, payment method, account details and first-rent due date. A new bank account is not automatically the agreed payment method; changing the payment manner requires agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for written confirmation** from the agency and owner that:
   - the agency has ceased acting;
   - the owner is now managing the tenancy;
   - the owner’s full name and address for service; and
   - the urgent-repairs emergency telephone number.  
   These are the details the owner must provide when there is no agent, and changes must be notified in writing within 7 days. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Independently verify the new account details** with the owner or agency using contact details already appearing in your signed lease—not merely by replying to the message containing the new bank details. The retrieved documents do **not** prescribe a bank-account verification procedure or say how to authenticate a changed account, so they do not answer that issue further.

4. **Ask for written confirmation of which payment method you are agreeing to use and any costs**, because the provider must tell you about costs associated with a particular payment method before you consent to use it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Keep the request, confirmation and proof of payment**, and request a rent receipt if needed. For a non-personal payment, if you request a receipt when paying, it must be provided within **5 business days**; the receipt must state your name and premises, date, period covered, amount and that it is rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

6. **Check your bond separately**: the owner or agent must lodge it with the RTBA within **10 business days** after receiving it. The RTBA should send you a receipt; if you have not received one within **15 business days** after paying the bond, contact the RTBA at **rtba@justice.vic.gov.au** or **1300 137 164**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three required points are covered. The hardest one, the payment-change point, is met by the answer's statements that "changing the payment manner requires agreement" and that the renter should "Independently verify the new account details with the owner or agency using contact details already appearing in your signed lease." The answer also covers the 7-day written notice of the owner's name, address for service and emergency repairs number, and the RTBA bond lodgement and receipt check.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never suggests withholding rent, and it requires notice and confirmation, stating that the rental provider "must give you written notice of the change in the relevant information within 7 days" and that "changing the payment manner requires agreement."

version-cited.reason: Yes - the answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101 (in force from 7 September 2022)' (link 97-109aa101) and relies otherwise only on 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002 (in force from 1 June 2022)' (link 21-3sra002), both of which were in force on 8 November 2022, and it draws on no other version.

[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the manual bank transfer is genuinely available and does not incur an additional fee, the documents support the view that the agent may offer card payment with a fee **provided the fee-free bank-transfer option is reasonably available**. ## What the renter can do or ask

You can ask the agent to confirm, in writing:

1. that the manual bank-transfer option is available **without any additional cost**;
2. the exact amount and basis of the card fee;
3. whether the fee is charged by the app company, the agent, or another party; and
4. when and how the fee was disclosed before you agreed to use the card-payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

If the bank-transfer option is not reasonably available, or the fee was not disclosed before consent, raise that with the agent and ask for a fee-free payment method. The retrieved documents do not contain a procedure or outcome for challenging or recovering a disputed card fee.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019**—the version in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Because you had **not entered into possession**, section 226 allowed you to terminate the tenancy by giving the landlord a **notice of termination** if the premises:

- were **not in good repair**;
- were **unfit for human habitation**;
- were unsafe;
- were not vacant;
- were not legally available as a residence; or
- were otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Damp, mould and rotting timber may support the “not in good repair” or “unfit for human habitation” grounds, but the documents do not say precisely when those conditions meet either test. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had to ensure that, on the agreed occupation day, the premises were **vacant and reasonably clean**; you were not required to enter premises that did not meet that requirement, and rent was not payable for the period before you actually entered into occupation if that requirement was not met. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord had a continuing duty to maintain the premises in **good repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Terminate before moving in.**  
   Give the landlord a written notice of termination under **section 226**, stating that you have not entered into possession and relying on the premises being not in good repair and/or unfit for human habitation. Section 226 is the statutory route; the documents do not describe this as an automatic cancellation merely because you found defects. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs instead.**  
   Notify the landlord in writing, describe and photograph the damp, mould and rotting timber, and ask for the repairs. For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord does not repair within **14 days** after written notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate; after receiving the Director’s report, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

   If the rotting timber or other defect makes the premises **unsafe**, it may fall within “urgent repairs”, because urgent repairs included work needed to remedy a fault or damage making rented premises unsafe or insecure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask for lower rent.**  
   You can ask the landlord to agree to a lower rent while the defects remain. The Act also allowed an application about **excessive rent**: the Tribunal could consider the premises’ state of repair and general condition when deciding what rent should reasonably be paid, and could order a refund of the difference from the date of your application. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not state that rent was automatically reduced merely because defects were discovered before occupation.

Keep the notice, inspection records, photographs, condition report and all communications. Do not simply stop paying or treat the lease as ended without giving the statutory notice or obtaining the landlord’s agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer says s 226 allows notice of termination before possession if the premises are 'not in good repair' or 'unfit for human habitation'. (2) It states the landlord's 'continuing duty to maintain the premises in good repair', describes requesting repairs, and notes that defects making the premises 'unsafe' may be 'urgent repairs'. (3) For the hardest point, it ties termination to 'relying on the premises being not in good repair and/or unfit for human habitation', treats the 'vacant and reasonably clean' requirement as a separate matter, and names photographs and inspection records as evidence.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer relies only on 2019-era duties such as "good repair", "unfit for human habitation" and "vacant and reasonably clean" without claiming the rental minimum standards or mould and damp standard applied, and it never says the renter must move in and pay rent; instead it says "you were not required to enter premises that did not meet that requirement" and offers termination "under section 226".

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019" and relies only on that in-force version. Its rules (s 226 termination before possession, vacant and reasonably clean premises, the 14-day non-urgent repair process, urgent repairs limited to unsafe or insecure faults, and excessive rent) do not apply the not-yet-in-force 2018 amendments, such as rental minimum standards or mould/damp as an urgent repair.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **Tuesday 8 November 2022**, the applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101 (7 September 2022)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002 (1 June 2022)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The lease should identify the rental provider and, if applicable, the agent. The prescribed form says the rental provider must notify you within **7 days** if that information changes. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) If there is no longer an agent, the rental provider must give you their full name, address for service and an emergency telephone number; if an agent remains, you must receive the agent’s identifying and contact details. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

Rent is payable using the method specified in the agreement. The rental provider and renter may change that method **by agreement**. A fee-free payment method must remain reasonably available, and you must be told about costs associated with a particular payment method before consenting to use it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** specifically prescribe a bank-account verification process for a changed rent account.

## What you can do or ask before paying

1. **Check the signed lease**: confirm the named rental provider, the agent’s details and the payment method or bank details recorded in it. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for written confirmation** from the agency and owner that:
   - the owner is now managing the tenancy;
   - the owner’s full legal name, address for service and emergency contact details are correct; and
   - the new account is the account to which rent is to be paid.  
   These details are relevant because the Act requires written information about the provider or agent and written notice of changes to that information. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

3. **If they say the tenancy rights and duties have been transferred**, ask for the required assignment/transfer notice. Where a rental provider assigns or transfers those rights and duties and a bond has been paid, the provider and transferee must notify the Authority using an approved form, signed by both, within **5 days** after the transfer takes effect, and give you a copy. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Do not pay the bond again.** The provider must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within **10 business days** after receiving it. The Authority must issue a receipt within **7 days** after receiving it; if you do not receive a receipt within **15 business days** after giving the bond to the provider, you may notify the Authority. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The prescribed form gives the RTBA contact details as **rtba@justice.vic.gov.au** and **1300 137 164**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Keep proof of every payment and request a rent receipt.** A rent receipt must state your name and premises, date, period covered, amount and that it is rent; if you request a receipt for a payment not made in person, it must be provided within **5 business days** of receipt. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

If the requested change is only a change of manager, the documents do not say that you must sign a new lease. If the new bank details cannot be confirmed against the provider/agent information and the signed agreement, the documents do not contain enough information to say that the account is genuine—so ask for written confirmation before paying.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The output covers all three points: the provider's full name, address for service, emergency telephone number and 7-day change notice; bond lodgement with the RTBA within 10 business days and checking for the Authority's receipt; and, for the hardest point, that the payment method may be changed 'by agreement', with the renter told to 'Ask for written confirmation from the agency and owner that... the new account is the account to which rent is to be paid' before paying.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter may stop paying rent or that details can change without notice; it says the payment method may change only "by agreement" and advises to "ask for written confirmation before paying" into the new account.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101 (7 September 2022)' (link 97-109aa101), and its only other source is the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002 (1 June 2022)' (link 21-3sra002); both were in force on 8 November 2022, and no other version is relied on.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **3 December 2025**, the relevant versions are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111** (in force from 25 November 2025). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005** (in force from 25 November 2025). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must ensure that smoke alarms are correctly installed, working, powered with batteries, and tested at least every 12 months. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed rental-agreement terms say the rental provider may enter to comply with duties under the Act, and that the renter **must allow entry where the proper procedure has been followed**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) They do **not** say that the renter must personally be home to let the inspector in, and the retrieved documents do not state that entry cannot occur using the agent’s key. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents also contain **no provision about a $90 rebooking fee**, or a fee for the renter not being home for a smoke-alarm check. Therefore, they do not establish that the agent can charge you that amount. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can write to the agent saying that you will not be home, but that you permit the properly notified inspection to proceed using the agent’s key. Ask them to confirm in writing that:

1. the inspector will attend during the stated weekday time window; and  
2. they will not charge the $90 fee.

If they insist on charging it, ask them to identify the specific legal or contractual provision authorising the charge. The retrieved documents do not provide one. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

It never says that entry to carry out the landlord's duty needs at least 24 hours' written notice, made within 8 am to 6 pm, or that the seven days' notice given satisfies this. It only refers vaguely to a 'properly notified inspection'. The first point is covered: the renter 'must allow entry where the proper procedure has been followed', and the documents 'do not say that the renter must personally be home'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts neither failing claim. On attendance it says the prescribed terms 'do **not** say that the renter must personally be home to let the inspector in.' On the fee it says the documents 'do not establish that the agent can charge you that amount.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111" and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005", each in force from 25 November 2025 and linked as 97-109aa111 and 21-3sra005, and it relies on no other version.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says — 15 January 2026

The applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, dated 25 November 2025** (“the Act”), in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005, dated 25 November 2025** (“the Regulations”), in force on 15 January 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent must ensure that a rent-payment method with **no additional cost**—apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account—is **reasonably available**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) A fee-free manual bank transfer appears capable of satisfying that requirement, although the documents do not define precisely what “reasonably available” means. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The provider or agent must also tell the renter about costs, including **third-party transaction fees** and electronic-payment-facility fees, **before** the renter agrees to use that payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The Act prohibits a person from demanding or receiving a charge for the **establishment or use of a direct-debit facility or any other electronic payment facility for paying rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do not state whether a card transaction surcharge of the kind described is legally treated as a charge for the “establishment or use” of the facility, rather than a payment surcharge.

The newer provision that would prescribe **“rent payment”** as a prohibited fee expressly excludes “payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act”, but that regulation only takes effect on **31 March 2026**, not on 15 January 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The documents therefore do not establish a separate, definitive ban on this card surcharge as at 15 January 2026.

### Does it matter who receives the fee?

The documents do **not** say that the result changes merely because the fee is paid to the payments company rather than the agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The obligation to provide a fee-free method and disclose third-party transaction fees is imposed on the residential rental provider or the provider’s agent, while the prohibition in section 51(3) applies to **“a person”**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) On the retrieved material, the payments company’s involvement does not by itself avoid those requirements, but the documents do not decide whether the particular company’s card fee is prohibited.

## What the renter can do or ask

You can ask the agent to confirm:

1. that the manual bank-transfer option is available as a genuinely fee-free rent-payment method; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
2. the amount and nature of the card fee, including whether it is a third-party transaction fee; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
3. when and how that fee was disclosed to you before you agreed to use the app; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
4. whether the fee is for establishing or using the electronic payment facility, which section 51(3) prohibits. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

If the fee-free transfer is not reasonably available, or the fee was not disclosed before you consented to the app, you can raise that with the agent and ask for the card fee to be removed or refunded. The retrieved documents do not specify a further complaint procedure or determine whether a refund must be made.

On the fee-free method, the answer says a method with "no additional cost—apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter's own bank account—is reasonably available" and that the fee-free manual bank transfer "appears capable of satisfying that requirement." On the hardest point, it says the provision prescribing "rent payment" as a prohibited fee "only takes effect on 31 March 2026, not on 15 January 2026."

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088**, incorporating amendments as at **2 July 2019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Because you have **not entered into possession**, section 226 allows the tenancy agreement to terminate if you give the landlord a **notice of termination** stating that the premises:

- are **not in good repair**;
- are **unfit for human habitation**;
- do not meet rental minimum standards; or
- are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord must ensure that the premises are maintained in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) On the agreed occupation day, the premises must also be vacant and reasonably clean; you are not required to enter premises that do not meet that requirement, and you do not have to pay rent for the period before you actually enter into occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do not specifically say whether particular damp, mould or rotting timber automatically makes premises “unfit for human habitation” or “not in good repair”; that would depend on the condition and seriousness of the defects. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask to terminate/cancel the agreement.**  
   You can give a written notice of termination under section 226, relying on the premises being not in good repair, unfit for habitation, below minimum standards, or otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) This is a statutory termination notice, rather than simply treating the lease as cancelled without notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask the landlord to repair the defects.**  
   Give written notice describing the damp, mould and rotting timber and request repairs. The landlord has a duty to maintain the premises in good repair. question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **8 November 2022**, the applicable documents were:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101, in force from 7 September 2022** (“rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002, in force from 1 June 2022** (“rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf”). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rent must be paid at the place and in the manner specified in the residential rental agreement. The rental provider and renter may change the manner of payment **by agreement**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) Therefore, a new bank account is not automatically binding merely because the agent emailed new details; the documents do not state a special procedure for changing bank-account details. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The agreement must identify the rental provider and, if applicable, the agent. The rental provider must notify the renter within **7 days** if any of those details change. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The provider or agent must also:

- make a **fee-free payment method** reasonably available, apart from fees charged by your own bank; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- permit payment by **Centrepay** and any prescribed payment method; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- tell you about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, dishonour fees or electronic-payment-facility fees, **before** you consent to that payment method; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- give a rent receipt within **5 business days** if you request one when making a non-personal payment. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

Your bond is separate from rent. The provider must lodge it with the RTBA within **10 business days** after receiving it. The RTBA should issue a receipt within **7 days** of receiving the bond; if you have not received a receipt within **15 business days** after paying it, you may contact the RTBA. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you should ask or check

Before paying the new account, ask for written confirmation of:

1. **Who the current rental provider and managing agent are**, including the changed name, address, phone number and email address. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **That the owner has taken over management** and that the new account is the account to be used for rent under your agreement.
3. **The effective date** of the change and the rent period covered by your next payment.
4. **Any payment fees**, and confirmation that a fee-free method remains available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
5. A rent receipt after payment if you request one. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

Compare the proposed payment method with the payment details in your signed agreement. The retrieved documents do **not** specifically require the agent to verify new bank details in any particular way, nor do they provide a specific anti-fraud procedure. If the change is not adequately confirmed, the documents do not say that you must pay into the new account merely on the basis of the message.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The hardest point, the rental provider's notice of details and of changes within 7 days, is covered by "The agreement must identify the rental provider and, if applicable, the agent. The rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if any of those details change," and the checklist adds the provider's name, address, phone and email. The emergency repairs number is not listed, but the substance of the point is unchanged. The bond point is covered: lodgement with the RTBA within 10 business days and contacting the RTBA if no receipt arrives. The payment point is covered: a change to the manner of payment is made by agreement, and the renter should get written confirmation before paying, which is a reasonable verification step.

The answer never says the renter may stop paying rent; its closest statement, "the documents do not say that you must pay into the new account merely on the basis of the message," concerns which account to pay into, not withholding rent. It also never says details can change without notice, stating instead that the manner of payment may change "by agreement" and that the provider "must notify the renter within 7 days" of changed details.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
Based on the following documents in force on your question date (3 December 2025):
*   ***Residential Tenancies Act 1997***, Authorised Version No. 111 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
*   ***Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021***, Authorised Version No. 005 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

Here is the answer to your questions:

### 1. Do you have to be there yourself to let the inspector in?
**No.** Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v111), a rental provider or their agent has the right to enter your home to carry out statutory duties, such as testing smoke alarms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Notice Period:** The agent must provide you with at least **24 hours' written notice** for this type of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
*   **Permitted Hours:** Entry is legally allowed between **8 a.m. and 6 p.m.** on any day (except public holidays) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
*   **Your Presence:** The law places a duty on you to "permit" the agent to enter the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It does not require your physical presence to unlock the door, especially since your agent already holds a key. As long as they provide proper notice and enter within the legal time window, they can use their key to access the property without you being there.

### 2. Can they charge you a $90 fee to rebook?
**The provided legal documents do not contain information regarding fees for rescheduling or rebooking routine inspections.** 
*   The Act explicitly prohibits rental providers from demanding or receiving fees for certain specific actions, such as giving consent to an assignment or subletting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
*   However, because the text is completely silent on inspection rebooking fees, the documents do not provide a direct answer to whether this $90 charge is lawful. You would need to review your specific residential rental agreement or seek further guidance from Consumer Affairs Victoria to determine if this fee is enforceable under your tenancy terms.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says the law 'places a duty on you to "permit" the agent to enter' and that the agent 'can use their key to access the property without you being there.' It also calls smoke alarm testing one of the rental provider's 'statutory duties' that requires 'at least 24 hours' written notice' between '8 a.m. and 6 p.m.', which by clear implication the seven days' notice satisfies.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says 'No' to needing to be home ('It does not require your physical presence to unlock the door'), and it never says the $90 must be paid, stating only that 'the documents do not provide a direct answer to whether this $90 charge is lawful.'

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111' (link 97-109aa111) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005' (link 21-3sra005), and applies no rule from any other version.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Vic), Authorised Version No. 111, which was in force on 15 January 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf):

**What the law says about your situation**
* **A free payment option must be available:** Your landlord or agent is legally required to ensure that a rent payment method with *no additional costs* (other than standard bank fees payable on your account) is "reasonably available" to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Since you have a manual bank transfer option with no fee, this requirement appears to be met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
* **You must be informed beforehand:** Your landlord or agent must give you information about any costs you may incur—including third-party transaction fees—*before* you consent to use that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
* **Who receives the fee is irrelevant:** The law does not distinguish based on who pockets the surcharge (whether it goes to the payments app company or the agent) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Its focus is strictly on whether *you* are forced to pay extra and whether a genuinely free alternative is accessible [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**
* **Confirm you were properly informed:** If your agent did not explicitly tell you about the card fee before you agreed to use the app, they may be failing their legal obligation to disclose costs beforehand [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). You can ask them to provide this information in writing.
* **Verify the free option is accessible:** Ensure the no-fee bank transfer is genuinely "reasonably available" and not artificially difficult to access or overly cumbersome [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If it is, you can ask your agent to make the free payment method easier to use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
* **Use the free method:** You are legally entitled to pay your rent via the no-cost bank transfer without penalty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

*(Note: This information applies specifically to Victorian residential tenancies as of 15 January 2026.)*

The first point is covered: 'a rent payment method with no additional costs... is reasonably available... Since you have a manual bank transfer option with no fee, this requirement appears to be met.'
