question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent gave me written notice seven days ahead that I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. The agent has a key to the place. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
# Smoke alarm check: entry notice and the $90 fee

**Documents used (in force on 3 December 2025):**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", **Authorised Version No. 111**, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf". The retrieved text doesn't print an Authorised Version number, but its metadata lists version 005, in force 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

**The notice looks valid.**
- A rental provider or their agent may enter between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday. For a purpose under s 86(1)(c), they must give at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Section 86(1)(c) covers entry needed to carry out a duty under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The provider has a duty to ensure smoke alarms work, have batteries, and are tested at least every 12 months (s 68AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm check therefore appears to fall under s 86(1)(c). That is my reading, because the Act doesn't say so in terms.
- Seven days' written notice exceeds the 24-hour minimum, and a weekday window of 10 am to 12:30 pm is within 8 am to 6 pm [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must be in writing, state why the agent wants to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. (s 88) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be there?**
- The documents don't say a renter must be present. The right given is to "enter rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Your duty is to "permit" a person exercising a right of entry in accordance with the Division to enter (s 89(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard-form summary says you must allow entry where the rental provider has followed proper procedure [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The retrieved text doesn't say whether an agent may use their own key to enter while you are out. I can't confirm that from these documents.
- Entry must be in a reasonable manner, and the person must not stay longer than necessary without your consent (s 87) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Can they charge $90?**
- Nothing in the retrieved Act or Regulations authorises a "rebooking fee" for a missed entry appointment.
- The charges the Act does address include key money and similar charges (s 51) and certain application and rent payment fees (s 51A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). None of these mentions a rebooking fee, so the documents neither allow nor expressly prohibit it.
- The smoke alarm testing duty sits with the rental provider, not the renter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent in writing** which provision lets them charge $90. The retrieved documents don't show one.
- **Ask whether presence is required.** If not, you can let entry happen without you. You can also agree a different time. Entry is allowed "at any time agreed with the renter" if you consent within 7 days before the entry (s 85(a)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal for an order limiting entry times.** You can do this under s 89(2)–(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **If the agent enters without following the Division,** you can apply to the Tribunal for an order restraining entry for a specified period (s 91) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entering otherwise than in accordance with the Division, without reasonable excuse, is an offence (s 91A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Limits of this answer:** I found nothing in the retrieved documents on whether the fee is lawful in itself, or on whether your lease has an additional term about it. Check your own agreement. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenants' advice service can confirm the fee point.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. For the presence point, the answer says 'The documents don't say a renter must be present' and that the renter's duty is to 'permit' entry (s 89(1)). This is the hardest point, because the answer hedges on whether the agent may use their own key and tells the renter to ask whether presence is required. Still, the rubric accepts 'the documents do not require it,' so it counts. For the duty and notice point, the answer says testing smoke alarms is the rental provider's duty (s 68AA). It says entry to carry out a duty needs at least 24 hours' written notice within 8 am to 6 pm, and that the seven days given satisfies this.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must be home or must pay the fee: it states "The documents don't say a renter must be present" and "Nothing in the retrieved Act or Regulations authorises a 'rebooking fee' for a missed entry appointment."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "Authorised Version No. 111" (link 97-109aa111) and the Regulations as "version 005" (file rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, link 21-3sra005), both the versions in force on 3 December 2025, and it relies on no other version.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. The app is run by a payments company my agent uses, and it's that company that charges the card fee. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## Short answer

On 15 January 2026, the documents I retrieved do not say outright that a card fee on a rent app is banned or allowed. The rules point in different directions on this. The fee-free bank transfer matters, and so does who receives the fee, but not in a simple way.

**Documents relied on:**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf". The metadata labels it version 111, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 June 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf". The metadata labels it version 005, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

I found no separate "Authorised Version" number in the text. The version numbers above come from the metadata. Both documents were in force on 15 January 2026.

## What the law says

- **A free payment method must be reasonably available.** The rental provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Bank fees or account fees on your own account don't count as additional costs (s 42(4)). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Fees must be disclosed first.** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using a particular payment method before you consent to it. This expressly includes third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees (s 42(7)). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Electronic fund transfers must be permitted.** Under s 42(5), the agent must permit prescribed payment methods, and the regulations prescribe electronic funds transfer (reg 19). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The standard rental agreement form also notes that a fee-free method must be permitted. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
- **Some charges are banned outright.** Under s 51(3)(b), "a person" must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The Act doesn't say whether a card-payment surcharge counts as a charge for using an "electronic payment facility". That is the main uncertainty. Section 42(7) also treats "third party transaction fees" as something a renter may incur, which suggests some fees may be allowed if disclosed. The documents don't reconcile the two provisions.
- **Slowness is not addressed.** The documents don't say whether a free method that is slower is still "reasonably available". I can't say that a slow free option does or doesn't satisfy s 42(4).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **Section 42 binds the agent.** It applies to the provider or their agent, so the agent must ensure a free option exists and must disclose fees, even if a payments company runs the app. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Section 51(3) applies to "a person".** It doesn't distinguish between the agent and the app company. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Section 51A targets third parties.** A business other than the provider, the provider's agent or a bank must not demand or receive a fee for a "prescribed matter" relating to payment of rent. That is aimed at a third-party company like your app provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Section 51A is not yet operative on your date.** The prescribed matters are in regulation 21C, which includes "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)". Reg 21C only has effect on and after 31 March 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) So the documents don't show this prohibition applying on 15 January 2026. After that date it would matter whether the fee goes to the third-party company. The documents don't say which "other Act" permits surcharges.

## What you can do

1. **Use the bank transfer.** It has no fee, and EFT is a method the agent must permit. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask the agent in writing** to confirm the card fee and who receives it. They must tell you about these costs before you consent to the method (s 42(7)). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
3. **Ask the agent to confirm a fee-free method is reasonably available** under s 42(4). Say if the slower transfer causes you real problems, such as late-rent risk. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
4. **Query the fee under s 51(3)(b).** Ask the agent why a charge for using an electronic payment facility is permitted. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
5. **Check the rules again after 31 March 2026.** The regulations on third-party rent payment fees start then. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Note too that the regulations version I found was in force only until 9 February 2026.

The documents don't cover complaint routes or whether this particular fee is lawful, so you may want to check with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says a no-additional-cost method must be 'reasonably available' (s 42(4)) and leaves open that the slower bank transfer may satisfy this ('I can't say that a slow free option does or doesn't satisfy s 42(4)'), while recommending that transfer. It also states that 'Reg 21C only has effect on and after 31 March 2026', so the third-party fee ban does not apply on 15 January 2026.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says neither, stating that reg 21C "only has effect on and after 31 March 2026. So the documents don't show this prohibition applying on 15 January 2026," and affirming that "The rental provider or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you" (s 42(4)).

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 111" (file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", link 97-109aa111) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 005" (file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf", link 21-3sra005), both in force on 15 January 2026, and it applies no rule from any other version (reg 21C comes from version 005 and is correctly noted as not yet in effect).

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. I haven't moved any of my things in or stayed there yet. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Source:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088 (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf"). It incorporates amendments as at 2 July 2019 and was in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), so it covers 15 October 2019.

The same file ends with amending-Act text that uses "renter", "residential rental provider", "rental minimum standards" and lists "mould or damp" as urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I haven't relied on that text. It isn't part of the operative sections of this version, and the retrieved text doesn't say it applied on 15 October 2019.

## What the law says

- **Before possession:** A tenancy agreement terminates if the tenant has not entered into possession and gives the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair", "unfit for human habitation" or "for any other reason unavailable for occupation" (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Landlord's repair duty:** The landlord must keep the premises "in good repair" (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition on the move-in day:** The landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed occupation day. A tenant need not enter if they aren't, and owes no rent from the agreed day until actually entering (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That section covers vacancy and cleanliness. The retrieved text doesn't say it extends to damp, mould or rot.

## Your options

**1. Cancel the lease**
- Section 226 fits your facts if you give written notice to the landlord. Its grounds are that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for habitation, or are otherwise unavailable for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The notice must be given before you enter into possession.
- The documents don't define "entered into possession", so I can't say whether collecting the keys counts. Don't move in or stay there, and keep evidence such as photos and dates.
- If you had already moved in, s 238 would let you give notice of intention to vacate where the premises are unfit for human habitation. The termination date can be the day you give notice or later [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Outside s 226 and s 238, a general notice of intention to vacate needs at least 28 days (s 235). For a fixed-term lease it has no effect if it names a date before the end of the term (s 236) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can also end the lease by agreement with the landlord (s 217) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs:** These include a serious roof leak and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure. The listed items in this version don't expressly include mould, damp or rotting timber [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For urgent repairs you can arrange them yourself if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to act and can't. You must give 14 days' written notice of the work and its cost. The landlord must reimburse the lesser of the reasonable cost or $1,000 (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal for an order, which must be heard within 2 business days, if you can't meet the cost, it exceeds $1,000, or the landlord refuses to pay (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give the landlord written notice. If the landlord hasn't done the repairs within 14 days, you can ask the Director to investigate (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can then apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the Director's report, or earlier if no report arrives within 90 days of your request (s 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can order specified repairs within a set time (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account:** After giving notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into this account while the landlord fails to repair (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** If you paid a bond, the landlord must give you two copies of a signed condition report before you move in. Within 3 business days of entering you must return one copy, signed or endorsed to show any disagreement (s 35) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition, except for matters you disagree with or defects not reasonably discoverable on inspection (s 36) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents give no clear right to a rent reduction because of defects you found before moving in.
- You can complain to the Director that rent is excessive because the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services or facilities, or because you received a rent increase notice (s 45) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Neither fits your situation as described.
- If the Tribunal does consider whether rent is excessive, it can look at the state of repair and general condition of the premises (s 47(3)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- A reduction would therefore have to be negotiated with the landlord, or a payment arrangement agreed.

The documents don't say which option is best for you. If the landlord disputes your notice, the Tribunal is the forum to resolve it. I'd get advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service before sending a termination notice.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered. Section 226 lets a tenant who has not entered possession terminate by notice where the premises are 'not in good repair' or 'unfit for human habitation'. Section 68 requires the landlord to keep the premises in good repair, repair requests are explained, and urgent repairs include 'any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure'. The hardest point is met because the answer separates s 65's vacancy/cleanliness duty from the s 226 disrepair/unfitness grounds and advises keeping 'evidence such as photos and dates'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer mentions "rental minimum standards" and "mould or damp" only to set them aside ("I haven't relied on that text... the retrieved text doesn't say it applied on 15 October 2019"), and it never says the renter must move in and pay rent; it instead advises cancelling under s 226 and says "Don't move in or stay there."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088' (file 'rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf', in force 2 July to 3 December 2019). It applies only rules from that version's operative sections (ss 35, 36, 45, 47, 65, 68, 72–77, 217, 226, 235, 236, 238), and it explicitly declines to rely on the not-yet-in-operation amending text, such as mould or damp as an urgent repair.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now, a week after I signed, the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Before paying, check that you have received written notice of the change, that the new payment method is agreed in writing, and that you will get receipts.

**Documents used (both in force on 8 November 2022):**
- *rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 7 September 2022 and listed as version 101. It was in force from 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- *rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, dated 1 June 2022 and listed as version 002 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

The retrieved text does not show an "Authorised Version No." label, so those version numbers come from the document metadata.

## What the law says

- **Notice of the change.** If an agent acts for the owner, the owner must give you the agent's details in writing. If there is no agent, the owner must give you their full name, an address for service of documents and an emergency phone number. The owner must give you written notice of any change in that information before the end of 7 days after the change (s 66(2)–(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The standard lease form carries the same note: the provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the agent or provider details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Changing how rent is paid.** Rent is payable in the manner specified in your agreement (s 42(2)). The provider and renter "by agreement" may change that manner (s 42(6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The standard form has a "Payment details" section in the agreement itself [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents do not say the owner or agent can change the account by notice alone.
- **Cost-free payment.** The owner or agent must make a payment method with no extra costs reasonably available, other than your own bank fees, and must permit electronic funds transfer (s 42(4)–(5); Regulation 19) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). They must also tell you about any costs of a payment method before you agree to it (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts.** Whoever receives your rent must give a written receipt immediately if you pay in person. If you don't pay in person, they must give one within 5 business days of receiving the payment, if you ask for it when you pay. The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that it is rent (s 43) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Records.** If no receipt is required, the receiver must keep a record for 12 months. They must give you a copy within 5 business days of your request (s 43(2)–(2A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the written notice.** Check that the owner's full name, address for service and emergency number have been given to you in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for the new payment details in writing and agree to the change.** Look at the "Payment details" in your lease [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A change to how rent is paid should be by agreement (s 42(6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask about costs.** Ask what fees, if any, the new method involves, and for a fee-free option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for a receipt each time you pay.** Request it when you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Check the bond.** Whoever received it (the agent included) must lodge it with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of receiving it, and holds it on trust until then (ss 404, 406, 408). The Authority must send you a receipt within 7 days of getting it (s 407). If you have no receipt within 15 business days of giving the bond, you can notify the Authority (s 409) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The lease form gives the Authority's contact details as rtba@justice.vic.gov.au and 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

If the owner took over the lease by assignment or transfer, the owner must notify the Authority within 5 days and give you a copy of that notice (s 424) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether an owner taking over management from an agent counts as a transfer.

## What the documents don't cover

The documents don't say how to confirm the new bank details are genuine, or what happens if you pay into an account that turns out to be wrong. As a practical step that does not come from the documents, you could confirm the change by contacting the owner and agent using the contact details in your signed lease, not the ones in the new message.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The s 66 written notice of the owner's full name, address for service and emergency phone number, plus notice of changes within 7 days. (2) Bond lodgement with the RTBA and the Authority's receipt (ss 406, 407). (3) Rent payment changes being 'by agreement' (s 42(6)). The hardest one, verifying through a known contact, is covered by 'you could confirm the change by contacting the owner and agent using the contact details in your signed lease, not the ones in the new message.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter can stop paying rent; it says the reverse of the second claim, that a change to how rent is paid "should be by agreement (s 42(6))" and that "the documents do not say the owner or agent can change the account by notice alone."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer identifies the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 101' (file rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, link 97-109aa101, dated 7 September 2022) and the Regulations as 'version 002' (21-3sra002, dated 1 June 2022), both in force on 8 November 2022, and every rule it applies comes from these versions.
